items: For EACH party pair and EACH act: did Δ act with PURPOSE, or with KNOWLEDGE TO A SUBSTANTIAL CERTAINTY? If yes, run the INTENTIONAL TORTS. If no, ask whether the thing or activity is in a strict-liability category — animal, food, ultrahazardous. If yes, run STRICT LIABILITY and plead negligence in the alternative. If no, run NEGLIGENCE.
Run all three if the facts support it. One act can be a battery AND negligence. If strict liability fails on a caveat, fall back to negligence — and say so.

sections.h: READ THE CALL OF THE QUESTION
items: The call determines what you write. If it asks whether a claim CAN BE ESTABLISHED, or whether a party WILL PREVAIL — walk the elements of the cause of action, then any affirmative defenses.
If the call is limited to ONE ELEMENT — cause in fact, for example — write ONLY that element.
FORMAT: 40–50 multiple choice on a scantron, plus 4–5 short-answer essays typed. No points off for improper structure on this exam; poor writing costs points on the final.
INTENT = a conscious purpose to cause the tort, OR knowledge to a substantial certainty that the tort will occur.

Modifiers: a child is capable of intent depending on AGE. An insane person is capable if able to intend THE ACT in question. Mistake as to target — wrong person, wrong animal — does NOT negate intent. Voluntary intoxication does NOT negate intent. TRANSFERRED INTENT transfers between persons AND between causes of action.

sections.h: A-1 — Which intentional tort? Sort by what Δ's act caused
items: BATTERY — contact with π's body or an item connected to it: (1) volitional act; (2) intent to cause harmful or offensive contact; (3) causation, DIRECT OR INDIRECT (poison, trap, thrown object); (4) harmful or offensive contact; (5) with the person of π — body plus connected items: purse, cane, plate. Complete UPON CONTACT. CROSSOVER: intent to assault that lands as contact = battery.

ASSAULT — apprehension, no touch: (1) volitional act; (2) intent; (3) causation; (4) apprehension = EXPECTATION, fear NOT required; (5) IMMINENT contact; (6) APPARENT ABILITY to make or cause contact. CROSSOVER: intent to batter that lands as apprehension = assault.

FALSE IMPRISONMENT — confinement in a bounded space: (1) volitional act; (2) intent to confine; (3) bounded space — how large? argue it; (4) physical restraint NOT required — threats to π, to π's property, or to a third person, or abuse of authority; (5) no apparent escape, OR escape poses risk of harm; (6) π AWARE of the confinement OR suffered injury. Complete upon confinement with awareness or harm.

IIED — severe distress from outrageous conduct: (1) act OR SERIES of acts; (2) intentional OR RECKLESS — the only tort here that accepts recklessness; (3) EXTREME AND OUTRAGEOUS: beyond all possible bounds of decency, atrocious and utterly intolerable in a civilized society — character and vulnerability of the victim is a FACTOR; threats of future physical violence may suffice; harm to a family member in π's presence may suffice IF Δ knew π was present and related; (4) causation; (5) SEVERE distress — a severely disabling emotional response; with a pre-existing condition, the EXACERBATION must be severe.

TRESPASS TO LAND — entry onto real property: (1) volitional act — only THE ACT need be intended, NOT the tortious result; (2) causes intrusion by a person or PHYSICAL SUBSTANCE — NOT vibration (strict liability or nuisance), NOT odor or noise (nuisance); (3) interferes with π's right of EXCLUSIVE POSSESSION. The interference IS the injury — no harm to land required; harm only increases damages. Complete upon entry.

INTERFERENCE WITH A CHATTEL — how severe? Dispossession, damage, or impairment of use = TRESPASS TO CHATTELS; no dispossession, damage, or impairment = NO TORT. Damages: cost of repair, fair rental value, losses from impaired use. PERMANENT dispossession or SUBSTANTIAL destruction = CONVERSION; remedy is a FORCED SALE — Δ pays full value — plus incidental losses; equitable factors may be dispositive in close cases.

sections.h: A-2 — Affirmative defenses (Δ must PLEAD and PROVE; FRCP 8)
items: Defeats π's prima facie case if the jury believes it. Subject to dispositive motions — dismissal for failure to state a claim, summary judgment, judgment as a matter of law, judgment non obstante veredicto.

CONSENT — EXPRESS (words or writing), APPARENT (gesture or behavior judged by a reasonable person under all circumstances, in some cases silence), IMPLIED (found by the court from the nature of π's activity — contact sports). Defeated where π is not rational or competent (intoxication, insanity, minority); where SCOPE IS EXCEEDED; where obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence despite a duty to disclose. Illegal acts: SPLIT, state by state. Sports: covers conduct within the CUSTOMS of the sport, which may extend BEYOND the written rules. Δ's good faith or a good outcome will NOT cause a court to imply consent.

MEDICAL EMERGENCY EXCEPTION — all four: (a) the patient cannot consent (unconscious, incompetent, seriously intoxicated, mentally ill); (b) the condition risks serious harm if treatment is delayed; (c) a reasonable person would consent; (d) the provider has no reason to believe THIS patient would refuse.

SELF-DEFENSE — reasonable force against a threat of battery. NO privilege to RETALIATE. Privilege exists where Δ REASONABLY BELIEVES force is necessary, EVEN IF MISTAKEN. Insults, however vile, never create it. No need to wait for the actual battery. Only NECESSARY force. RETREAT IS REQUIRED IN FRANKLIN AND AT COMMON LAW — EXCEPT INSIDE ONE'S HOME, where retreat is never required. Doubts resolved in favor of Δ.

DEFENSE OF OTHERS — one may defend another where that person could defend himself. The privilege is DERIVATIVE and governed by the same rules. MISTAKE: courts divided. IN FRANKLIN, the intervenor is privileged even when mistaken about the attack, PROVIDED he acted in GOOD FAITH.

DEFENSE OF PROPERTY — NEVER deadly force to protect property alone. No mechanical device or dog may do what you could not do yourself. No privilege where the entry is LAWFUL (meter reader, postal carrier). Unlawful entry into an OCCUPIED HOME is a threat to the occupants — different rules, Castle Doctrine. 'Get off my lawn or I'll shoot' is only the law in movies.

RECAPTURE OF CHATTELS — the rightful possessor may use NON-DEADLY force, after a demand is ignored, OR where he reasonably believes demand would be useless, OR reasonably believes substantial harm will be done to the chattel before demand can be made; AND he reasonably believes force is the only way to recover it.

SHOPKEEPER'S PRIVILEGE — upon REASONABLE SUSPICION goods were taken, REASONABLE never deadly force, to detain ON the premises, for a REASONABLE TIME to investigate. 'Reasonable' is for the court in the first instance, then the jury.

PUBLIC NECESSITY — a defense to ALL the intentional torts studied. Property destroyed or tortious conduct committed where NECESSARY or APPARENTLY necessary to prevent greater harm to the community. NO compensation at common law (many states now provide it by statute). Private rights are subordinate to the safety of the community. Includes quarantine and other restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery. IN PRACTICE: public necessity is almost always PUBLIC PROPERTY or QUARANTINE protecting PUBLIC HEALTH — for most other circumstances, look to JUSTIFICATION.

PRIVATE NECESSITY — a defense to trespass to land and the other intentional torts. Property may be used or taken to avoid greater harm to persons or other property. NO legal wrong is committed, so the owner MAY NOT compel the user to desist; NO NOMINAL DAMAGES. The user MUST PAY the value of any damage; no punitives. If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results, THE OWNER IS LIABLE.
AUTHORITY OF LAW AND DISCIPLINE — now mostly statutory (parental, teacher). Know the common law rules exist, but LOOK FOR A STATUTE.

JUSTIFICATION — a catch-all; a privilege may arise in circumstances not anticipated. The test is a measure of NECESSITY (the concept, not the defense) under those particular circumstances. The categories of privilege are not closed.

sections.h: B — Strict liability: liability without fault
items: FRAMING: some things and activities are so fraught with peril that public policy demands those who use, possess, sell, or undertake them pay for all harm done, EVEN IF they exercised all possible care.

CONTAMINATED FOOD — π must plead and prove: (1) Δ was in the BUSINESS of manufacturing or selling the food product; (2) the product was CONTAMINATED — poison, putrefaction, or foreign object, NOT 'bones and stones' natural to the food; (3) it reached π in SUBSTANTIALLY THE SAME CONDITION as when it left Δ's control; (4) the contamination was a cause; (5) of injury suffered by π.

WILD ANIMALS — (1) Δ owned, kept, or harbored a wild animal: 'wild' means NOT BY CUSTOM DEVOTED TO THE SERVICE OF MANKIND at the TIME and in the PLACE where kept, and Δ must have been the LAST to keep or harbor it; (2) that TYPE of animal has dangerous or vicious propensities arising from its WILDNESS — SCIENTER IS PRESUMED; (3) the animal, AS A RESULT OF ITS WILDNESS, caused; (4) harm to π's person or property.

UNUSUALLY DANGEROUS DOMESTIC ANIMALS — usually pets: (1) Δ kept, possessed, or harbored it, need NOT own; (2) it was ABNORMALLY DANGEROUS, usually from previous attacks on people or other animals or other risk-creating behavior; (3) SCIENTER: ACTUAL OR CONSTRUCTIVE knowledge — NOT PRESUMED, the key difference from wild animals; (4) the animal, AS A RESULT OF ITS ABNORMAL DANGEROUSNESS, caused; (5) harm to π's person or property.
CAVEAT FOR BOTH ANIMAL TRACKS: if the harm came from some OTHER characteristic — not wildness, not dangerousness — strict liability WILL NOT LIE. Another cause of action, such as negligence, might.

ULTRAHAZARDOUS ACTIVITIES — (1) Δ undertook the activity; (2) the activity WAS ultrahazardous (run the 520 factors); (3) one or more of the RISKS that make it ultrahazardous — blasting: concussion of air, vibration of ground, flying debris; (4) caused; (5) harm to π.

§ 519: one who carries on an abnormally dangerous activity is subject to liability for harm to the person, land, or chattels of another resulting from the activity, ALTHOUGH HE HAS EXERCISED THE UTMOST CARE to prevent the harm. (2) Limited to the KIND OF HARM the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous.

§ 520 — FACTORS, NOT ELEMENTS (say this). Be able to reproduce (a), (b), (c); the full list is not required. (a) a high degree of risk of some harm to person, land, or chattels of others; (b) likelihood that the resulting harm will be GREAT — 'likelihood' does NOT mean probability; (c) INABILITY TO ELIMINATE THE RISK BY THE EXERCISE OF REASONABLE CARE — THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FACTOR; (d) not a matter of common usage; (e) inappropriateness to the PLACE; (f) value to the community outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
DEFENSE: at common law, only VOLUNTARY ASSUMPTION OF A KNOWN RISK is a complete defense to strict liability.
ALWAYS STATE THE GENERAL DUTY — 'a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances.' This must be in your answer.

STEP 1 — WHO is this Δ? Physical limitation: reasonable person WITH that limitation. Low IQ: ordinary reasonable person, no allowance. Insane: ordinary reasonable person. Lacking knowledge: ordinary reasonable person. SUPERIOR knowledge: MUST USE IT. Professional or special skill: professional standard. Child: child standard.

PROFESSIONAL STANDARD — must POSSESS AND EXERCISE the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession or occupation IN GOOD STANDING. EXPERT TESTIMONY generally necessary, and the expert must be familiar with the professional standard AND with the case before the court. Physician, medical specialist, attorney, pilot, electrician. PHYSICIANS: the standard is NATIONAL — THE OLD LOCALITY RULE IS OUT IN FRANKLIN. A physician's duty INCLUDES INFORMED CONSENT.

INFORMED CONSENT — usually invoked where treatment WAS properly performed within the standard of care but the patient had an adverse outcome anyway. The duty is to inform, BEFORE the patient consents, that the adverse outcome is a risk even if treatment is properly performed; to disclose facts and risks MATERIAL to the patient's decision; measured in FRANKLIN by what would be material to a REASONABLE PATIENT in the same situation. Failure to inform is handled as NEGLIGENCE, not battery.

CHILDREN AS Δs — duty is to act as a reasonably prudent child of like AGE, EDUCATION, INTELLIGENCE, and EXPERIENCE. This is an OBJECTIVE standard: based on children with similar characteristics, NOT on this particular child. Dangerous activities generally reserved for adults get the ADULT standard; there is no clear rule, so look at the thing the child is using — tractor, snowmobile, GUN on one side; small toys, ball, bicycle on the other. GUN: ADULT STANDARD.

STEP 2 — WHERE does the SPECIFIC CONTENT come from? Name a source; do not leave duty generic. COMMON SENSE / common or local knowledge — the way things are done by people who do this activity regularly (building haystacks). CUSTOM of an industry or trade and STANDARDS of a profession — the duty the industry imposes on ITSELF, formally or informally; admissible through EXPERT TESTIMONY; does NOT bind court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it; MAY BE CHALLENGED on Hand Formula considerations. CASE LAW — an earlier case may bind us depending on its value as precedent. STATUTE / REGULATION / ORDINANCE → negligence per se.

FORESEEABLE NEGLIGENCE OF ANOTHER TORTFEASOR — sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another: barriers at a roadside site because negligent driving is foreseeable; lighting in a parking lot where crime or negligent backing-out is foreseeable; a landlord's security — locks, cameras — based on foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place. THE EXTENT OF THE DUTY DEPENDS ON THE RISK.

NO OBVIOUS SOURCE → REVERSE-ENGINEER: review the sequence from Δ's conduct to π's harm; determine what Δ could have done differently to prevent or minimize it; that conduct — to do or refrain from — is the possible duty; its cost is the COST OF AVOIDANCE under Hand.
Applies where a statute, regulation, or ordinance is intended (1) to protect a CLASS OF PERSONS including π, AND (2) from the TYPE OF INJURY suffered by π. BOTH ARE REQUIRED.

IF BOTH MET: the court BORROWS that standard as the negligence duty; NPS BINDS THE JURY ON DUTY AND BREACH; cause in fact must STILL be separately proven; proximate cause is rarely an issue because by the nature of NPS π is a foreseeable π suffering foreseeable harm.

CHECK FOR AN EXCUSE — may, but need not, be built into the statute, or adopted from § 288A: (a) reasonable because of the actor's INCAPACITY; (b) he neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance; (c) unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply; (d) confronted by an EMERGENCY not due to his own misconduct; (e) COMPLIANCE WOULD INVOLVE A GREATER RISK OF HARM — the MOST IMPORTANT excuse.

IF ONLY ONE PRONG MET — NPS CANNOT BE APPLIED: treat the cause of action as COMMON LAW NEGLIGENCE; the statute may still be a useful SOURCE OF IDEAS for the content of duty but need not be adopted 'per se'; breach, cause in fact, and proximate cause apply as they ordinarily would.

sections.h: C-1 — THE HAND FORMULA and the overlays
items: Place yourself metaphorically at the place where, and the time just before, the conduct took place. NO HINDSIGHT. Weigh (1) the LIKELIHOOD, as understood THEN, that SOME harm would occur, and (2) the LIKELY SEVERITY of that harm should it occur — together THE RISK — against (3) the COST OF AVOIDING it, including the cost to THIS Δ, to OTHERS SIMILARLY SITUATED, and the SOCIAL COSTS of imposing the duty.

FAIRNESS: this is NOT arithmetic, it is SOCIAL POLICY — say so. It requires comparing incommensurables. Hand himself says it is both INEFFICIENT and UNFAIR to impose a cost of avoidance too high for the risk. So even with risk AND a measurable cost of avoidance, THERE MIGHT STILL BE NO DUTY.

OFFENSIVE USE: Hand can ATTACK an industry custom or professional standard as an inadequate duty in light of the risk — Helling: very small likelihood, very high severity, vanishingly low cost of avoidance; the profession imposed no duty on itself; the court imposed it AS A MATTER OF LAW.

FORESEEABLE HARM — a duty will be imposed where harm of a certain type is foreseeable 'to the eye of ordinary vigilance,' sometimes including harm not directly caused by the initial breach but foreseeable in itself or as to which Δ is 'held to the knowledge.' EGGSHELL π: same general TYPE, MORE SEVERE — Δ still liable. PSYCHOLOGICAL HARM is ALWAYS foreseeable when π suffers physical harm, and Δ is liable for ALL of it even if unforeseeably severe.

EMERGENCY (protects Δs) — the law does not hold one in an emergency to the mature judgment required where there is opportunity for deliberate action; he is not required to exercise unerring judgment. NOT available if Δ created the emergency.

RESCUE (makes πs) — 'Danger invites rescue.' A duty RUNS TO THE RESCUER, often the same duty owed the primary π. Cause in fact and proximate cause must both be established, but it is rare that harm to a rescuer is held too remote. A RESCUER MAY SUE THE PERSON RESCUED if that person is at fault for creating the risk.
Usually a matter of common sense once the duty has been defined, and usually a question of fact for the jury. Sometimes an inference is necessary.

HAZARD / INSPECTION CASES — were inspections made frequently enough? Did an inadequate schedule cause the injury? π HAS THE BURDEN. Δ is liable if Δ (a) CREATED the hazard, (b) had ACTUAL knowledge, or (c) had CONSTRUCTIVE knowledge — based on the CONDITION of the hazard (brown banana peels) or the TIME BETWEEN INSPECTIONS.

RES IPSA LOQUITUR — (1) no direct evidence of precisely how the negligent act happened; (2) the accident does not normally occur absent negligent conduct by someone; (3) the instrumentality of injury was within Δ's EXCLUSIVE CONTROL. EFFECT: establishes breach FOR PURPOSES OF THE PRIMA FACIE CASE ONLY — it gets π to the jury on duty and breach, does NOT bind the jury to accept the inference, and CAUSATION MUST BE PROVEN SEPARATELY.
π BEARS THE BURDEN: evidence such that a reasonable jury could believe the breach MORE LIKELY THAN NOT caused the harm for which THIS π sues. Need not be quantifiable, and very often is not.
IMPACT CASES — often obvious: breach causes impact, impact causes injury. State it briefly.

WHERE EVENTS ARE NOT QUANTIFIABLE — enough to say the breach 'greatly multiplies the chances of accident to the plaintiff, and is of a character naturally leading to its occurrence.' An inference the jury MAY reach. Unlit staircase with no handrail: the jury may find the breach caused the fall even though others did not fall and π might have fallen anyway. ABSENCE OF A SAFETY DEVICE may be inferred to be the cause in fact where the device is intended for precisely that purpose. But testimony insufficient to support ANY inference — 'I don't remember' — FAILS.
MULTIPLE POSSIBLE CAUSES — π establishes three possible causes, all attributable to Δ, with no other possible causes; as to none can it be said it is more likely than not. π STILL GETS TO THE JURY.
Δ BEARS NO BURDEN OF PROOF — Δ's expert need not establish Δ's explanation; the testimony is intended to dissuade the jury from accepting π's inference and is admissible as rebuttal.

SCIENCE — in chemical exposure cases where the harm also occurs in nature: π must prove the EXPOSURE occurred, and that the exposure caused HER injury, not merely that it CAN in general cause this type of injury. EPIDEMIOLOGICAL EVIDENCE: the incidence in the EXPOSED population must be MORE THAN DOUBLE the incidence in a similar UNEXPOSED population — 10 per 100,000 unexposed means AT LEAST 21 per 100,000 exposed. MEDICAL MALPRACTICE: the physician's negligence must more likely than not have caused the death or loss, INCLUDING loss of a chance of a better outcome.

LOST CHANCE — usually med mal, theoretically not limited to it. The physician's negligence must more likely than not have caused the death or other loss. Where the chance of survival was LESS THAN 50%, LOSS is RECHARACTERIZED to include the loss of the chance of survival. 75% chance: the estate reaches the jury on DEATH itself. 40% chance: the estate cannot prove the breach caused the death, so the harm is the lost 40% chance.

CONCURRENT CAUSES — more than one breach by more than one Δ causing the same injury; breaches that together cause harm neither could alone; more than one breach where only one could have caused it and we cannot know which; or more than one cause any of which alone would have sufficed, sometimes including non-culpable causes.

MULTIPLE POSSIBLE CAUSES — (1) independent tortfeasors, only ONE could have caused the harm [Summers v. Tice]: JOINT AND SEVERAL. (2) independent tortfeasors whose negligence HAD TO COMBINE, no harm without the combination [Hill v. Edmonds]: JOINT AND SEVERAL. (3) causes some culpable and some not, any of which alone would have caused the harm — lightning fire and RR fire: joint and several among those legally culpable, NOT Mother Nature; if only one Δ is culpable, 100% LIABILITY.

JOINT AND SEVERAL LIABILITY — JOINT: π may recover the TOTAL judgment from ANY ONE Δ; each is liable for the full amount. SEVERAL: after π is paid in full, a Δ who paid more than its proportional share (presumed EQUAL at common law) may recover from the other Δs to bring everyone even — the RIGHT OF CONTRIBUTION.

ENTERPRISE vs. MARKET SHARE — often chemical and pharmaceutical exposure. Predicate for both: all Δs breached the SAME duty in the SAME manner; any one or any combination could have caused this π's harm; it must have been one or some, but we cannot know which. ENTERPRISE: ALL industry members before the court → JOINT AND SEVERAL. MARKET SHARE: not all, but the MAJORITY of the market, before the court → SEVERAL liability only. Causation in fact must STILL be proven.

THE FOUR CASE PATTERNS — PERKINS: quantification possible but not developed by π (π loses). REYNOLDS: no quantification possible; itemize the claim — absence of light and handrail caused the fall, or so the jury could infer (π reaches the jury). GENTRY: testimony supports no inference at all, 'I don't remember' (π loses). KRAMER: quantification possible and it shows more likely than not CANNOT be established (π loses).

Damages: cost of repair, fair rental value, and losses caused by impairment of use
model: Elements: (1) a volitional act; (2) causes; (3) interference with π's right of exclusive possession of the chattel by dispossession of the chattel, damage to the chattel, or impairment of use of the chattel.

The dispossession, damage, or impairment constitutes the tort: no dispossession, damage, or impairment, no tort. Damages are measured by the cost of repair, fair rental value, and losses caused by impairment of use, depending on the facts of the case.

components: Volitional act
Causes
Interference with π's right of exclusive possession of the chattel by
Permanent dispossession, OR
Substantial destruction
Such as would warrant payment by Δ of the full value of the chattel to the rightful possessor
This is in effect a FORCED SALE
Incidental losses also recoverable
Equitable factors might be dispositive in close cases
model: Elements: (1) a volitional act; (2) causes; (3) interference with π's right of exclusive possession of the chattel by permanent dispossession or substantial destruction, such as would warrant payment by Δ of the full value of the chattel to the rightful possessor.
The remedy is in effect a forced sale — Δ pays full value. Incidental losses are also recoverable, and equitable factors might be dispositive in close cases.

components: Must be pleaded and proved by Δ
Defeats π's prima facie case if believed by the jury
Subject to dispositive motions: dismissal for failure to state a claim, summary judgment, judgment as a matter of law, judgment non obstante veredicto
See FRCP 8

The list: consent, self-defense, defense of others, defense of property, recapture of property, shopkeeper's privilege, public necessity, private necessity, authority of law, discipline, justification
model: Affirmative defenses must be pleaded and proved by Δ, and defeat π's prima facie case if believed by the jury. They are subject to dispositive motions — dismissal for failure to state a claim, summary judgment, judgment as a matter of law, and judgment non obstante veredicto. See FRCP 8.

The defenses studied: consent; self-defense; defense of others; defense of property, recapture of property, and the shopkeeper's privilege; public necessity; private necessity; authority of law and discipline; and justification.

components: Express: a clear expression of specific consent, spoken or in writing
Apparent: a gesture or behavior indicating consent as understood by a reasonable person under all the circumstances, in some cases including silence
Implied: found by the court based on the nature of π's activities, such as contact sports
Must be the act of a rational, competent person — intoxication, insanity, minority may invalidate
Scope of consent may not be exceeded
Invalid if obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence where there is a duty to disclose
Consent to illegal acts may or may not be a good defense — state by state
Limited to conduct within the customs of the sport or activity, which may go beyond the rules of the game
Δ's good faith or a good result will not cause a court to imply consent
model: Consent may be express, apparent, or implied. EXPRESS: a clear expression of specific consent, spoken or in writing, to contact, confinement, or other conduct by Δ that would otherwise be tortious. APPARENT: a gesture or behavior by π communicating or otherwise indicating consent, as it would be understood by a reasonable person under all the circumstances, including in some cases π's silence. IMPLIED: consent found by the court based on the nature of π's activities, such as participation in contact sports.

Consent must be the act of a rational, competent person; intoxication, insanity, and minority may invalidate it. The scope of consent may not be exceeded. It is invalid if obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence concerning a matter as to which there is a duty to disclose — consent is vitiated by failure to disclose information material to the consent. Consent to illegal acts may or may not be a good defense, state by state.

Consent is limited to contact or otherwise tortious activity within the customs of the sport or activity, which may go beyond the rules of the game, and may be implied from local usage and custom. Δ's good faith, or a good result, will not be a basis for a court to imply consent.

components: Anyone may use reasonable force to defend self against a threat of battery
No privilege to retaliate
Privilege present when Δ reasonably believes force is necessary, EVEN IF Δ IS MISTAKEN
Insults, however vile, never create the privilege
No need to wait for the actual battery
Only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged
RETREAT IS REQUIRED IN FRANKLIN AND AT COMMON LAW
EXCEPT INSIDE ONE'S HOME, where retreat is never required
Doubts generally resolved in favor of Δ
model: Anyone may use reasonable force to defend himself against a threat of battery. There is no privilege to retaliate. The privilege is present where Δ reasonably believes the use of force in self-defense is necessary, even if Δ is mistaken. Insults, however vile, never create a privilege to use force. There is no need to wait for an actual battery. Only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged.
RETREAT: retreat is required in Franklin and at common law. The exception is inside one's own home, where retreat is not required. Doubts are generally resolved in favor of Δ.
Note that many other states have moved away from a retreat requirement outside the home, but Franklin has not — apply the Franklin rule.

components: One may defend another in circumstances in which that person would be privileged to defend himself or herself
The privilege is DERIVED from the other's privilege
The intervenor's conduct is governed by all the same rules that govern the victim's conduct in self-defense
Mistake: courts are divided
IN FRANKLIN: the intervenor's privilege is present even when mistaken as to the attack, PROVIDED the intervenor acted in good faith
model: One may defend another in circumstances in which that person would be privileged to defend himself or herself. The privilege is derived from the other's privilege to defend him or herself, and the intervenor's conduct is governed by all the same rules that govern the victim's conduct in cases of self-defense — a consequence of its derivative character.

On mistake, courts are divided. The rule in the State of Franklin is that the intervenor's privilege is present even when the intervenor is mistaken as to the attack on the other, provided the intervenor has acted in good faith.

components: Deadly force may NEVER be used to protect property alone
One may not use a mechanical device or dog to do what one could not do oneself
No privilege to use force if the intrusion onto property is lawful — meter reader, postal carrier
Unlawful entry into an OCCUPIED HOME is treated as a threat to the occupiers
That is conceptually different, governed by different rules — Castle Doctrine
'Get off my lawn or I'll shoot' is only the law in movies
model: Deadly force may not be used to protect property. One may not use a mechanical device or a dog to do what one could not do oneself. There is no privilege to use force if the intrusion onto the property is lawful — a meter reader or a postal carrier, for example.

Unlawful entry into an occupied home is treated as a threat to the occupiers. That is conceptually different and governed by different rules; the Castle Doctrine applies there. 'Get off my lawn or I'll shoot' is only the law in movies.

components: The rightful possessor may use NON-DEADLY force to recapture the chattel, AND
After a demand for return is ignored; OR
The RP reasonably believes such demand would be useless; OR
The RP reasonably believes substantial harm will be done to the chattel before demand can be made; AND
The RP reasonably believes the chattel can be recovered only by use of such force
model: The rightful possessor of a chattel may use non-deadly force to recapture it, after a demand for return is ignored, or where the rightful possessor reasonably believes such a demand would be useless, or reasonably believes substantial harm will be done to the chattel before a demand can be made — and in every case only where the rightful possessor reasonably believes the chattel can be recovered only by the use of such force.

components: A specific iteration of the common law right to recapture chattels
Regulated by statute in most states; we care only about the common law form
Upon reasonable suspicion that a customer has taken goods
Use reasonable force — never deadly — to detain the customer ON the premises
For a reasonable time to investigate
What is reasonable is for the court in the first instance, then for the jury
model: The shopkeeper's privilege is a specific iteration of the common law right to recapture chattels. It is regulated by statute in most states, but only the common law form concerns us.

A retail merchant may, upon reasonable suspicion that a customer has taken goods, use reasonable force — never deadly — to detain the customer on the premises, for a reasonable time to investigate. The determination of what is reasonable is for the court in the first instance, then for the jury.

components: A defense to ALL the intentional torts studied
Property may be destroyed, or otherwise tortious conduct committed
When necessary, or APPARENTLY necessary, to prevent greater harm to the community
No compensation required at common law
Many states have provided for compensation by statute
Private property rights and other individual rights are subordinate to the safety of society
Includes quarantine and other physical restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery
IN PRACTICE: public necessity is almost always about protecting PUBLIC PROPERTY, or quarantine protecting PUBLIC HEALTH
For most other circumstances, look toward JUSTIFICATION instead
model: Public necessity is a defense to all the intentional torts studied. Property may be destroyed, or otherwise tortious conduct committed, when necessary or apparently necessary to prevent greater harm to the community.

No compensation is required at common law; the rationale in destruction of property cases may have been that this particular property would have been destroyed anyway. Many states have provided for compensation by statute. Private property rights and other individual rights are subordinate at common law to the safety of society and the community.
The principle includes quarantine and other physical restraints that would otherwise be false imprisonment or battery.

Sorting rule: public necessity is almost always about protecting public property, or quarantine protecting public health. For most other circumstances, look toward justification — the catch-all — rather than stretching public necessity.

components: A defense to trespass to real property and to the other intentional torts
Private property may be used or taken to avoid a greater harm to persons or other property
No legal wrong is committed, therefore the owner may not compel the user to desist
NO NOMINAL DAMAGES
The user must pay the value of any damage to the property
No punitive damages
If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, THE OWNER IS LIABLE
model: Private necessity is a defense to trespass to real property and to the other intentional torts. Private property may be used or taken in order to avoid a greater harm to persons or other property.

No legal wrong is committed thereby, and therefore the owner may not compel the user to desist. There are no nominal damages. The user must pay the value of any damage to the property, but there are no punitive damages.
If the owner forces the user to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is liable.

blurts.topic: Authority of law, discipline, and justification
components: Authority of law and discipline are now regulated mostly by statute
Many statutory changes to old common law rules — parental privilege to discipline children, teacher privilege to discipline students
Know the common law rules are out there, but in practice look for a statute
Justification is a catch-all concept
A privilege to commit an act otherwise tortious may arise in circumstances unanticipated before
The test in Sindle is simply a measure of necessity — the concept, not the defense
The categories of privilege are not carved in stone; the concept admits of flexibility
model: Authority of law and discipline are now regulated mostly by statute, with many statutory changes to the old common law rules — especially the parental privilege to discipline children and the teacher's privilege to discipline students. Know the common law rules are out there, but in practice look for a statute.

Justification is a catch-all concept: a privilege to commit an act or acts otherwise tortious may arise in various circumstances unanticipated before. The test in Sindle is simply a measure of necessity — the concept, not the defense — under those particular circumstances. The message is that the categories of privilege are not carved in stone for all time; the concept admits of flexibility.

components: Liability without fault
Some things and activities are so fraught with peril that public policy demands those who use, possess, sell, or undertake them pay for all harm done
Even if they have exercised all possible care
Contaminated food
Wild animals
Unusually dangerous domesticated animals
Ultrahazardous activities
model: Strict liability is liability without fault. Some things and activities are so fraught with peril that public policy demands that those who use, possess, sell, or otherwise undertake them should pay for all harm done in connection with the thing or activity, even if they have exercised all possible care.
The four categories: contaminated food; wild animals; unusually dangerous domesticated animals; and ultrahazardous activities.

components: Δ was engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food products at issue
The food product was contaminated — poison, putrefaction, or foreign objects in food
Not applied to harm caused by 'bones and stones' natural to the food
The food product reached the π-consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left Δ's control
The contamination of the product was a cause
Of injury suffered by π
model: To establish a prima facie case in strict liability for harm suffered as a result of ingesting contaminated food, π must plead and prove: (1) Δ was engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food products at issue; (2) the food product was contaminated — meaning poison, putrefaction, or foreign objects in food, and not applied to harm caused by bones and stones natural to the food; (3) the food product reached the π-consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left the manufacturer's or seller's control; (4) the contamination was a cause; and (5) of injury suffered by π.

components: Δ owned, kept, or harbored a wild animal
A wild animal is one NOT BY CUSTOM DEVOTED TO THE SERVICE OF MANKIND at the time and in the place in which it is kept
Δ must have been the LAST to have kept or harbored the animal
The type of animal has dangerous or vicious propensities arising from its wildness
Δ is held to the knowledge of such dangers: SCIENTER IS PRESUMED
The animal, as a result of its wildness, caused
Harm to π's person or property
model: To establish a prima facie case in strict liability against the owner, keeper, or harborer of a wild animal, π must prove: (1) Δ owned, kept, or harbored a wild animal — a wild animal being one not by custom devoted to the service of mankind at the time and in the place in which it is kept, and Δ must have been the last to have kept or harbored it; (2) the type of animal harbored by Δ has dangerous or vicious propensities arising from its wildness, as to which Δ is held to the knowledge, scienter being presumed; (3) the animal, as a result of its wildness, caused; (4) harm to π's person or property.
Caveat: if the harm was caused by some other characteristic of the animal, other than its wildness, strict liability will not lie, but another cause of action, such as negligence, might.

components: Usually these are pets
Δ kept, possessed, or harbored it — NEED NOT OWN
An abnormally dangerous domestic animal
Dangerousness usually arises from previous attacks on people or other animals, or other behavior that creates risk of harm
Scienter: Δ had ACTUAL OR CONSTRUCTIVE knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness
This is NOT presumed, as it is with wild animals
The animal, as a result of its abnormal dangerousness, caused
Harm to π's person or property
model: To establish a prima facie case in strict liability for an unusually dangerous domestic animal — usually a pet — π must prove: (1) Δ kept, possessed, or harbored it, and need not own it; (2) it was an abnormally dangerous domestic animal, a quality usually arising from previous attacks on people or other animals, or other behavior that creates a risk of harm; (3) scienter: Δ had actual or constructive knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness, which is not presumed as it is with wild animals; (4) the animal, as a result of its abnormal dangerousness, caused; (5) harm to π's person or property.
Caveat: if the harm was caused by some characteristic of the animal other than its dangerousness, strict liability will not lie, but another cause of action, such as negligence, might.

components: Δ undertook a certain activity
The activity was ultrahazardous — run the § 520 factors
One or more of the risks associated with the activity that make it ultrahazardous
For blasting: concussion of air, vibration of ground, and flying debris
Caused
Harm to π
model: To establish a prima facie case in strict liability for an ultrahazardous activity, π must prove: (1) Δ undertook a certain activity; (2) the activity was ultrahazardous; (3) one or more of the risks associated with the activity that make it ultrahazardous; (4) caused; (5) harm to π.
For blasting, those characteristic risks are concussion of air, vibration of the ground, and flying debris.

components: At common law, only VOLUNTARY ASSUMPTION OF A KNOWN RISK is a complete defense to claims for strict liability
model: At common law, only voluntary assumption of a known risk was considered to be a complete defense to claims for strict liability.

components: Duty
Breach
Cause in Fact
Proximate Cause
Harm
model: The elements of negligence: duty, breach, cause in fact, proximate cause, and harm.

components: A legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances
This is the general duty and MUST BE PART OF YOUR ANSWER
In addition, duty has a specific content based on the facts of the case
Sources: common sense; custom of an industry or trade; standards of a profession; statute, regulation, ordinance, or case law
model: Duty is a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances. This is the general duty, and it must be part of your answer.

In addition, in each case duty also has a specific content based on the facts of the case, and sometimes comes from identifiable sources: common sense; the custom of an industry or trade; the standards of a profession; and statute, regulation, ordinance, or case law.

components: As a matter of law, everyone is presumed to be the ordinary, reasonably prudent person, with caveats
Physical limitations: the duty of a reasonable wheelchair-bound, blind, or deaf person to others
Low IQ: duty of an ordinary, reasonable person
Insane: duty of an ordinary, reasonable person
Lacking knowledge: duty of an ordinary, reasonable person
Superior knowledge: MUST USE THAT KNOWLEDGE
Child: the child standard
Professional or special skill: the professional standard
model: As a matter of law, everyone is presumed to be the ordinary, reasonably prudent person, with the following caveats.
Physical limitations are accounted for: the duty of a reasonable wheelchair-bound person, or a reasonable blind or deaf person, to others.

Mental abilities or development generally are not. Low IQ: the duty of an ordinary, reasonable person. Insane: the duty of an ordinary, reasonable person. Lacking knowledge: the duty of an ordinary, reasonable person. Superior knowledge: must use that knowledge. Child: the child standard. Professional or special skill: the professional standard.

components: Duty is to act as a reasonably prudent child of like AGE, EDUCATION, INTELLIGENCE, EXPERIENCE
This is an OBJECTIVE standard
Based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child, NOT on this particular child
When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an ADULT standard
There is no clear rule for which activities qualify
Hint: look at the thing the child is using — tractor, snowmobile, gun; versus small toys, ball, bicycle
GUN: ADULT STANDARD
model: A child Δ's duty is to act as a reasonably prudent child of like age, education, intelligence, and experience. This is an objective standard, which means it is a general standard based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child, but it is not based on this particular child.

When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an adult standard. There is no clear rule for when an activity fits this category; the hint is to look at the thing the child is using — compare a tractor, snowmobile, or gun with small toys, a ball, or a bicycle. A gun is the adult standard.

blurts.topic: Sources of the content of duty
components: Common sense, common or local knowledge — the way things are done by people who do this activity regularly
Custom of an industry or trade, and standards of a profession
The duty a particular industry, trade, or profession imposes on ITSELF, formally or informally
Admissible in evidence through expert testimony
Does not bind court or jury but is important evidence; courts ordinarily follow it
May be challenged on Hand Formula considerations
Case law — an earlier case may bind us depending on its value as precedent
Statute, regulation, or ordinance — negligence per se
model: Common sense, common or local knowledge — the way things are done by people who do this activity, whatever it is, regularly, such as building haystacks.

Custom of an industry or trade, and standards of a profession: industries, trades, and professions generally set their own standards of conduct, either formally by what they agree to or informally by what they do. It is the duty a particular industry, trade, or profession imposes on itself. It is admissible in evidence through expert testimony. It does not bind the court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it. It may be challenged on the basis of Hand Formula considerations.

Case law: if an earlier case has imposed or declined to impose a duty, that case might bind us in future cases, depending on its value as precedent. Statute, regulation, or ordinance leads to negligence per se.

components: Applies where a statute, regulation, or ordinance is intended:
(1) to protect a class of persons INCLUDING π, AND
(2) from injury of the TYPE suffered by π
BOTH ARE REQUIRED
The court will 'borrow' the duty of conduct as the negligence duty
If applicable, NPS binds the jury on DUTY AND BREACH
May be inapplicable because the two-prong standard is not met, or because an excuse applies
Must also be a cause in fact of the harm
Must also be a proximate cause, but that is rarely an issue — π is a foreseeable π suffering foreseeable harm
model: Negligence per se applies where a statute, regulation, or ordinance is intended (1) to protect a class of persons including π, and (2) from injury of the type suffered by π. Both are required.

Where it applies, the court will borrow the duty of conduct from that source as the negligence duty, and negligence per se binds the jury on duty and breach. It may be inapplicable because the two-prong standard is not met, or because an excuse applies.

The violation must also be a cause in fact of the harm suffered by π. It must also be a proximate cause, but proximate cause is rarely an issue, because by the nature of negligence per se π is a foreseeable π suffering foreseeable harm.

components: A person who is a professional or has special skill must POSSESS AND EXERCISE the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession or occupation IN GOOD STANDING
Expert testimony is generally necessary
The expert must be familiar with the professional standard of care AND with the case before the court
E.g. physician, medical specialist (neurologist, psychiatrist, surgeon), attorney, pilot, electrician
For physicians the standard of care is NATIONAL — the old locality rule is OUT in Franklin
A physician's duty includes informed consent
model: A person who is a professional or has special skill is required to possess and exercise the knowledge and skill of an ordinary member of the profession or occupation in good standing.

Expert testimony is generally necessary, and the expert must be familiar with the professional standard of care and with the case before the court. Examples: physician, medical specialist such as a neurologist, psychiatrist, or surgeon; attorney; pilot; electrician.
For physicians the standard of care is national — the old locality rule is out in Franklin. A physician's duty includes informed consent.

components: Part of a physician's duty and standard of care
Usually invoked where treatment WAS properly performed within the standard of care but the patient had an adverse outcome anyway
The duty is to inform, BEFORE the patient gives consent, that the adverse outcome is a risk even if treatment is properly performed
The duty is to inform of facts and risks MATERIAL to the patient's decision
Measured in Franklin by what would be material to a REASONABLE PATIENT in the same situation as π
Failure to inform is handled as NEGLIGENCE, not battery
model: Informed consent is part of a physician's duty and standard of care. It is usually invoked in litigation where treatment was properly performed within the standard of care but the patient had an adverse outcome anyway.

The duty of the physician is to inform, before the patient gives consent to the procedure or medication, that the adverse outcome is a risk even if the treatment is properly performed. The duty is to inform of facts and risks material to the patient's decision, measured in Franklin by those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient.
Failure to inform may lead to liability, but is handled as negligence, not battery, in Franklin and generally in the US.

components: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another tortfeasor
A general contractor had a duty to put barriers up to protect workers on a roadside job site because negligent driving is foreseeable
Duty to have proper lighting in a parking lot where crimes or negligent driving are foreseeable
Duty of a landlord to provide security sufficient for the risk — locks, cameras
Based on foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place
The extent of the duty here depends on the risk
model: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another tortfeasor. A general contractor had a duty to put barriers up to protect workers on a roadside job site because negligent driving is foreseeable.

Other examples: a duty to have proper lighting in a parking lot where crimes or negligent driving — backing out of parking spaces — are foreseeable; and a landlord's duty to provide security sufficient for the risk, such as locks and cameras, based on the foreseeability of intentional torts and crimes in that place. The extent of the duty here depends on the risk.

blurts.topic: When there is no obvious source of duty
components: Odd or unfamiliar facts, or situations where the duty is not obvious, require a more elaborate approach
Review the sequence of facts leading from Δ's conduct to π's harm
Determine what Δ could have done differently that would have prevented or minimized the harm
This is reverse engineering the facts
Whatever conduct, to do or to refrain from, that would have prevented the harm is the conduct we consider as a possible duty
The cost of that conduct is the cost of avoidance under Learned Hand's formula
model: Odd or unfamiliar facts, or situations where the duty is not obvious, require a more elaborate approach. Review the sequence of facts leading from Δ's conduct to π's harm, and determine what Δ could have done differently that would have prevented or minimized the harm.

This is what is meant by reverse engineering the facts: whatever conduct, to do or to refrain from, that would have prevented the harm in this case, is the conduct we consider as a possible duty. Note that the cost of that conduct is the cost of avoidance that we consider under Learned Hand's formula.

components: Once we decide the conduct by Δ would have avoided the harm, we must decide whether it ought to be imposed as a legal duty
Put ourselves metaphorically at the place where, and at the time just before, the conduct took place
The likelihood, as we would have understood it THEN, that SOME harm would occur
The likely severity of that harm, should it occur
These together are THE RISK
Compare the risk to the cost of avoiding it by complying with the duty contemplated
The cost includes the cost to this Δ, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs of imposing the duty
THIS IS SOCIAL POLICY, NOT MATH
model: Once we decide the conduct by Δ would have avoided the harm, we must decide whether it ought to be imposed as a legal duty. To do so we put ourselves metaphorically at the place where, and at the time just before, the conduct took place.

We consider the likelihood, as we would have understood it then, that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur. These together are the risk. We then compare the risk to the cost of avoiding that risk and that harm by complying with the duty we contemplate. We consider the cost, including the cost to this Δ, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty. This is social policy, not math.

components: Comparing risk to cost of avoidance is not arithmetic; it's social policy
Unavoidably, it requires comparing incommensurables
Hand says it is both INEFFICIENT and UNFAIR to impose on Δs a cost of avoidance too high for the risk involved
So even if there is risk and a reasonably measurable cost of avoidance, there might still be NO DUTY
OFFENSIVE USE: Hand can be used to ATTACK a custom of an industry or a professional standard as an inadequate duty in light of the risk
In Helling: very small likelihood of harm, very high severity, vanishingly low cost of avoidance; the profession imposed no duty on itself; the court imposed the duty as a matter of law
WITH THE HAND FORMULA YOU CAN MAKE A POINT IN EITHER DIRECTION
Courts of equal standing, with very good judges, reach opposite results on the same facts
On an exam: argue both, then choose
model: We compare the risk to the cost of avoidance of that risk. This is not arithmetic; it is social policy, and unavoidably it requires comparing incommensurables. Judge Hand says so himself: it is both inefficient and unfair to impose on defendants a cost of avoidance too high for the risk involved. So even if there is risk and a reasonably measurable cost of avoidance, there might still be no duty.

Offensive use: Hand's formula can also be used to attack a custom of an industry or a professional standard as an inadequate duty in light of the risk. In Helling the issue was a duty to perform an ocular pressure test — a very small likelihood of harm, a very high likely severity if harm occurred, and a vanishingly low cost of avoidance — yet the profession did not impose the duty on itself. The court, applying a recognizable Hand approach, imposed the duty as a matter of law.

With the Hand formula you can make a point in either direction. Courts of equal standing, with very good judges, have reached opposite conclusions on materially identical facts — the classified-ad cases being the example, where one court found a duty and another, of equal standing in a different jurisdiction, found none. On an exam, argue both directions and then choose.

components: FORESEEABILITY IS UNAVOIDABLE IN A DUTY CASE — address it
A duty will be imposed when harm of a certain type is foreseeable 'to the eye of ordinary vigilance'
Sometimes this includes harm not directly caused by the initial breach
…but either foreseeable in itself, or as to which Δ is 'held to the knowledge'
EGGSHELL π: the harm is the same general TYPE as foreseeable but MORE SEVERE — Δ is still liable
Psychological harm is ALWAYS foreseeable when π suffers physical harm
Δ is liable for all of that psychological harm, even if unforeseeably severe
model: Foreseeability is unavoidable in a duty case. Whatever the source of the duty, the answer must engage with what was foreseeable — it runs through the Hand analysis, through the scope of the duty, and through the harm.

A duty will be imposed when harm of a certain type is foreseeable 'to the eye of ordinary vigilance.' Sometimes this includes harm not directly caused by the initial breach, but either foreseeable in itself or as to which Δ is 'held to the knowledge.'
Eggshell plaintiff: the harm that results is of the same general type as foreseeable, but is more severe than what was foreseeable. Δ remains liable.
Psychological harm is always foreseeable when π suffers physical harm, and Δ is liable for all the psychological harm, even if that harm is unforeseeably severe.

components: The law does not hold one in an emergency to the exercise of that mature judgment required where there is opportunity for deliberate action
He is not required to exercise unerring judgment
EMERGENCY PROTECTS Δs
Not available if Δ created the emergency
model: The law in this state does not hold one in an emergency to the exercise of that mature judgment required of him under circumstances where he has an opportunity for deliberate action. He is not required to exercise unerring judgment, which would be expected of him were he not confronted with an emergency requiring prompt action.

Note the pairing: emergency protects defendants; rescue makes plaintiffs. Example: Driver 1, proceeding lawfully, sees Driver 2 skidding toward him and accelerates to clear the point of entry rather than stopping. Impact follows. Driver 1 may be found not negligent due to the emergency created by Driver 2, even though stopping would have been the better response.

components: 'Danger invites rescue' — it is a natural impulse, not to be discouraged by the law
'The emergency begets the man. The wrongdoer may not have foreseen the coming of a deliverer. He is accountable as if he had.'
A duty RUNS TO THE RESCUER, often the same duty that ran to the primary π
Cause in fact and proximate cause must both be established
But it is rare that harm to the rescuer will be held too remote — policy favors protection of rescuers
A RESCUER MAY SUE THE PERSON RESCUED if that person is at fault for creating the risk
RESCUE MAKES πs
model: Danger invites rescue; it is a natural impulse, not to be discouraged by the law. The emergency begets the man; the wrongdoer may not have foreseen the coming of a deliverer, but he is accountable as if he had.

A duty runs to a rescuer, often the same duty that ran to the primary π. Cause in fact and proximate cause must both be established, but it is rare that the harm to the rescuer will be held too remote from Δ's breach of duty, because policy favors the protection of rescuers.
A rescuer may sue the person rescued, if that person is at fault for creating the risk.

components: Usually a matter of common sense once the duty has been defined
Usually a question of fact for the jury
Sometimes an inference is necessary
model: Breach is usually a matter of common sense once the duty has been defined, and is usually a question of fact for the jury. Sometimes an inference is necessary.

components: Duty to inspect where there is a dangerous condition or hazard of or on the land
Were inspections made frequently enough? Did an inadequate inspection schedule cause the injury?
π HAS THE BURDEN
Δ is liable if it CREATED the hazard
…or if it has ACTUAL knowledge of the hazard
…or if it has CONSTRUCTIVE knowledge of the hazard
Constructive knowledge based on the CONDITION of the hazard — brown banana peels
…or based on the TIME BETWEEN INSPECTIONS
model: Where there is a dangerous condition or hazard of or on the land, the questions are whether inspections were made frequently enough and whether an inadequate inspection schedule caused the injury. π has the burden.

Δ is liable if it created the hazard, if it has actual knowledge of the hazard, or if it has constructive knowledge of the hazard. Constructive knowledge may be based on the condition of the hazard — brown banana peels — or on the time between inspections.

components: The most important of the inferences
There is no direct evidence of precisely how the negligent act happened
The accident does not normally occur absent negligent conduct by someone
The instrumentality of injury was within Δ's EXCLUSIVE CONTROL
EFFECT: establishes breach of duty FOR PURPOSES OF THE PRIMA FACIE CASE ONLY
It gets π to the jury on duty and breach
It does NOT bind the jury to accept the inference
CAUSATION MUST BE PROVEN SEPARATELY
model: Res ipsa loquitur is the most important of the inferences. Its requirements: (1) there is no direct evidence of precisely how the negligent act happened; (2) the accident does not normally occur absent negligent conduct by someone; (3) the instrumentality of injury was within Δ's exclusive control.

Effect: it establishes breach of duty for purposes of the prima facie case only. In other words, it gets π to the jury on duty and breach, but it does not bind the jury to accept the inference. Causation must be proven separately.

Example: π buys a toaster oven. The third time he uses it, it bursts into flames, damaging his kitchen. The fire destroys so much of the oven that it is impossible to determine how the fire started. π may plead res ipsa loquitur to establish breach of the manufacturer's duty.

components: π BEARS THE BURDEN OF PROOF
The burden is to offer evidence such that a reasonable jury could believe the breach 'MORE LIKELY THAN NOT' caused the harm for which THIS π sues
This need not be quantifiable, and very often is not
Sometimes obvious, as in impact injury cases: breach causes impact, impact causes injury
model: π bears the burden of proof on cause in fact. The burden is to offer evidence such that a reasonable jury could believe that the breach more likely than not caused the harm for which this π sues. This need not be quantifiable, and very often is not.
Cause in fact is sometimes more obvious, as in impact injury cases: breach causes impact, impact causes injury. State it briefly and move on.

blurts.topic: Cause in fact — where events are not quantifiable
components: It is enough to say the breach 'greatly multiplies the chances of accident to the π, and is of a character naturally leading to its occurrence'
This is an inference the jury MAY permissibly reach
Staircase example: π falls at night on a staircase lacking lighting and a handrail
The jury may find the breach caused the fall, even though others did not fall and π might have fallen anyway
ABSENCE OF A SAFETY DEVICE may be inferred to be the cause in fact when the device is intended for precisely that purpose
Testimony insufficient to support any inference — 'I don't remember' — FAILS
model: Where the events are not quantifiable, it is enough to say that the breach greatly multiplies the chances of accident to the π, and is of a character naturally leading to its occurrence. This is an inference that the jury may permissibly reach.

Example: at night π falls down a railroad station staircase that lacked lighting and a handrail. The jury may find that the breach of the duty to have lighting and a handrail caused π's fall, even though others did not fall and π might have fallen even with those safety features present.

The absence of a safety device may be inferred to be the cause in fact of harm when the device would be intended for precisely that purpose — π could not remember why she fell, but remembered reaching for a handrail that was not there. By contrast, testimony insufficient to support any inference — 'I don't remember' — fails.

blurts.topic: Cause in fact — science and 'more likely than not'
components: In chemical exposure cases where the harm also occurs in nature, causation requires careful empirical analysis between natural and culpable causes
π must prove the EXPOSURE occurred
π must prove the exposure caused HER injury — not that it can in general cause this type of injury
π may offer EPIDEMIOLOGICAL EVIDENCE
Expert testimony that the incidence in the exposed population is MORE THAN DOUBLE the incidence in a similar unexposed population
Example: 10 per 100,000 unexposed → π must prove at least 21 per 100,000 exposed
MEDICAL MALPRACTICE: the physician's negligence must more likely than not have caused the death or loss, INCLUDING loss of a chance of a better outcome
model: In chemical exposure cases in which the harm alleged also occurs in nature, the determination of causation requires careful empirical analysis as between natural and culpable causes, to determine whether Δ or Nature caused this π's harm.

π must prove the exposure occurred, and must also prove that the exposure caused her injury — not that it can in general cause this type of injury. This is difficult where the manner in which the chemical acts within the human body is not known to science.

π may offer epidemiological evidence: expert testimony that the incidence of this type of harm in a population exposed to the drug or chemical is more than double the incidence in a similar unexposed population. Example: 10 incidents in an unexposed population of 100,000 means π must prove at least 21 incidents in an exposed population of 100,000.
In medical malpractice, the physician's negligence must, more likely than not, have caused the death or loss, including loss of a chance of a better outcome.

components: These are FACTORS to be considered, not elements of a cause of action
(a) Existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land or chattels of others
(b) Likelihood that the harm that results will be great — likelihood does NOT mean probability
(c) Inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care
(d) Extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage
(e) Inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on
(f) Extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes
model: In determining whether an activity is abnormally dangerous, the following factors are to be considered. These are not elements of a cause of action; they are factors to be considered — say so.

(a) Existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land or chattels of others; (b) likelihood that the harm that results from it will be great, where likelihood does not mean probability; (c) inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care; (d) extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage; (e) inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on; and (f) extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes — how much does the community benefit compared to the risk of harm?
Factors (d) and (e) are generally read together.

components: Usually arises in medical malpractice, but theoretically not limited to it
Med mal rule: the physician's negligence must more likely than not have caused the death or other loss
LOSS — the element of harm — IS RECHARACTERIZED
To include not only death, but LOSS OF THE CHANCE OF SURVIVAL
…when the chance of survival was LESS THAN 50%
75% chance case: estate reaches the jury on death itself, under more likely than not
40% chance case: the estate cannot prove the breach caused the DEATH, so the harm is recharacterized as the lost 40% chance
model: Lost chance usually becomes an issue in medical malpractice but is theoretically not limited to med mal. The med mal rule is that the physician's negligence must, more likely than not, have caused the death or other loss.
Where the chance of survival was less than 50%, loss — the element of harm — is recharacterized to include not only death but also the loss of the chance of survival.

Compare: a patient arrives in the emergency room with a 75% chance of survival with proper medical care after a heart attack; the doctor malpractices and the patient dies. Under the more likely than not standard, the estate gets to the jury on the claim that the breach of duty was the cause in fact of death.

A patient arrives with a 40% chance of survival with proper care; the doctor malpractices and the patient dies. The estate cannot prove the breach caused the death, because even with proper care she more likely than not would have died. What the estate can prove — virtually to a certainty — is that the malpractice caused the loss of that 40% chance, which is why the harm element is recharacterized.

components: Sometimes more than one breach by more than one Δ causes the same injury
Sometimes the breaches TOGETHER cause the harm, when either breach by itself could not have
Or there is more than one breach but only ONE could have caused the harm — and we don't know and can't know which
Or there is more than one cause and ANY of them would have caused the harm by itself
Sometimes the causes are not all culpable causes
model: Sometimes more than one breach by more than one Δ causes the same injury. Sometimes the breaches together cause the harm, when either breach by itself could not have. Or there is more than one breach but only one breach could have caused the harm, and we do not know and cannot know which. Or there is more than one cause and any of the causes would have caused the harm by itself — and sometimes the causes are not all culpable causes.

blurts.topic: Multiple possible causes — the three patterns
components: (1) Two or more INDEPENDENT tortfeasors, only ONE could have caused the harm [Summers v. Tice] — JOINT AND SEVERAL
(2) Two or more tortfeasors acting independently whose negligence HAD TO HAVE COMBINED to cause the harm — without the combination, no harm [Hill v. Edmonds] — JOINT AND SEVERAL
(3) Two or more causes, SOME CULPABLE SOME NOT, any of which alone would have caused the harm — lightning fire and railroad fire
In (3): joint and several as among those that can be legally culpable — not Mother Nature, not lightning
In (3): if only one Δ can be held culpable, 100% LIABILITY
model: Three patterns. First, two or more independent tortfeasors where only one could have caused the harm — Summers v. Tice — giving joint and several liability. Second, two or more tortfeasors acting independently whose negligence had to have combined in order to cause the harm, so that without their combined negligence there would be no harm — Hill v. Edmonds — also joint and several liability.

Third, two or more causes, some culpable and some not, any of which alone would have caused the harm — the lightning fire and the railroad fire. Liability is joint and several as among those that can be legally culpable; not Mother Nature, not lightning. If only one Δ can be held culpable, that Δ bears 100% liability.

components: Applies when two or more Δs are found liable to one π for harm caused by them all
Two consequences follow
THE JOINT PART: π may recover the TOTAL amount of the judgment from ANY ONE Δ — each is liable for the full amount
THE SEVERAL PART: after π is paid in full, a Δ who paid more than its proportional share may recover from the other Δs
Shares are presumed at common law to be EQUAL as among Δs
That right of recovery is called the RIGHT OF CONTRIBUTION
model: When two or more defendants are found liable to one π for harm caused by them all, two consequences follow.
The joint part: π may recover the total amount of his judgment from any one of the Δs — each Δ is liable to π for the full amount.

The several part: after π is paid in full, if any Δ has paid more than its proportional share — presumed at common law to be equal as among Δs — that Δ may recover from the other Δs as much as is necessary to bring everyone even with respect to their share of liability. That right of recovery is called the right of contribution.

components: Often, but not exclusively, applied in chemical and pharmaceutical exposure cases
ALL Δs breached the SAME duty in the SAME manner
Any one, or any combination of Δs, could have caused this π's harm
It must have been one or some of them, but we can't know which
ENTERPRISE: ALL industry members are before the court — JOINT AND SEVERAL liability
MARKET SHARE: NOT all industry members are before the court; the MAJORITY of the 'market' is — SEVERAL liability only
NB: causation in fact must still be proven as described in the earlier rules
model: Enterprise and market share liability are often, but not exclusively, applied in chemical and pharmaceutical exposure cases. The predicate is the same for both: all Δs breached the same duty in the same manner; any one, or any combination of Δs, could have caused this π's harm; it must have been one or some of them, but we cannot know which.
ENTERPRISE: all industry members are before the court, all at fault in the same manner — joint and several liability.
MARKET SHARE: not all industry members are before the court, but the majority of the market is, all at fault in the same manner — SEVERAL liability only.
Note that causation in fact must still be proven as described in the general rules.

cards.scenario: Δ's dog, which Δ knows has bitten twice before, escapes a gate Δ left unlatched and bites π. Which framework or frameworks should the answer run?
options: Strict liability only, since the dog is abnormally dangerous
Strict liability for the abnormally dangerous domestic animal, and negligence in the alternative for the unlatched gate
Negligence only, since Δ did not intend the bite
Battery, by transferred intent from the dog
cards.explanation: Run all three frameworks where the facts support them. The scienter and the animal's dangerousness support strict liability; the unlatched gate independently supports negligence. Plead negligence in the alternative rather than choosing.
cards.why: Sorting is not choosing — an answer that runs only one framework leaves points on the table.

cards.scenario: Δ's wild-caught fox, kept as a pet, knocks over a lamp with its tail and starts a fire that burns π's shed. Strict liability fails on the caveat. What should the answer do next?
options: Stop — the caveat ends the analysis
State that strict liability will not lie because the harm flowed from a characteristic other than the animal's wildness, then pivot expressly to negligence
Argue the fox was really a domestic animal
Run trespass to land against the fox's owner
cards.explanation: The caveat for both animal tracks is that where the harm was caused by some other characteristic of the animal, strict liability will not lie — but another cause of action, such as negligence, might. The answer should say so and pivot.
cards.why: TRICKY: the caveat is an invitation to switch frameworks, not a stopping point.

cards.scenario: Δ shoots at what he believes is a feral hog damaging his crops. It is π's prize sow. Is the intent element satisfied?
options: No — Δ intended to shoot a different animal
Yes — mistake as to target does not negate intent
No — Δ's purpose was to protect his crops
Yes — but only if Δ was negligent in identifying the animal
cards.explanation: Mistake as to target, whether the wrong animal or the wrong person, does not negate intent. Δ intended the act and its consequence; his error about which animal he was shooting is immaterial.
cards.why: Mistake goes to identity, not to purpose or volition.

cards.scenario: Δ drinks to the point of poor judgment and deliberately shoves π off a barstool. Δ argues intoxication negated intent. What result?
options: Intent negated — Δ could not form the requisite mental state
Intent established — voluntary intoxication does not negate intent
Intent negated unless Δ remembers the shove
Intent established only if Δ is a habitual drinker
cards.explanation: Voluntary intoxication does not negate intent. The shove was volitional and purposeful; the criminal law's treatment of specific intent does not carry over.
cards.why: One of the five modifiers stated flatly — no qualifiers to argue around.

cards.scenario: Δ swings a bat at A intending to strike him. A ducks; the bat strikes B, whom Δ never saw, and B had also seen it coming. Which doctrine supplies intent as to B, and for what?
options: None — Δ had no intent toward B
Transferred intent, which transfers both between persons and between causes of action, supporting battery against B and potentially assault as well
Transferred intent, but only between persons, so only battery
Res ipsa loquitur
cards.explanation: Intent transfers between persons and between causes of action. The intent to batter A supplies the intent element as to B, who was struck; and where the act intended to cause contact instead causes apprehension, that same intent supports assault.
cards.why: TRICKY: the doctrine runs on two axes, and (c) tests whether you know both.

cards.text: A {{volitional}} act intended to cause {{harmful}} or {{offensive}} contact with the {{person}} of the π, and which {{causes}} such contact.
cards.why: Tort is complete upon contact — no harm need be proved.

cards.scenario: Δ laces π's coffee with a drug. π drinks it hours later and is sickened. Δ argues he never touched π. What result?
options: No battery — Δ made no contact with π
Battery — causation may be direct or indirect, and poison is the classic indirect case
No battery — the delay breaks causation
Battery only if Δ handed π the cup
cards.explanation: Causation for battery may be direct or indirect; poison, a trap, and a thrown object are all sufficient. Δ need not lay hands on π.
cards.why: Indirect causation is expressly in the element — do not require a touch.

cards.scenario: Δ intends only to frighten π by swinging a stick close to his head. Δ misjudges and the stick strikes π. What result?
options: Assault only, since contact was not intended
Battery — the intent to commit an assault will support a judgment for battery where the act intended to cause apprehension instead results in contact
Neither, since Δ intended no contact
Battery only if Δ was reckless
cards.explanation: The relationship between the two torts runs both ways: the intent to commit an assault supports a judgment for battery if the act intended to cause apprehension results instead in contact, and the intent to commit a battery supports assault if the act intended to cause contact results instead in apprehension.
cards.why: TRICKY: the crossover is easy to state in one direction and forget in the other.

cards.scenario: Δ yanks a cane out of π's hand in anger. Δ never touches π's body and the cane is undamaged. Can π establish a prima facie case for battery?
options: No — contact must be with π's body
Yes — the person of π includes items connected to the body, such as a purse, a cane, or a plate
No — the proper claim is trespass to chattels only
Yes — but only if π suffered physical harm
cards.explanation: The element is contact with the person of π, which includes the body and items connected to the body. And because the tort is complete upon contact, no physical harm need be shown.
cards.why: A trespass to chattels claim may also lie, but it does not displace the battery.

cards.text: A {{volitional}} act intended to cause {{apprehension}} of harmful or offensive contact with the {{person}} of the π, and which causes such apprehension.
cards.why: Apprehension means expectation — fear is not necessary, though it may increase damages.

cards.scenario: Δ points an unloaded gun at π, who does not know it is unloaded and expects to be shot. Δ argues he could not possibly have caused contact. What result?
options: No assault — actual ability to cause contact is required
Assault — the element is apparent ability to make or cause contact, judged from π's position
No assault — π must prove fear
