Assault only if the gun was later found to be loaded
cards.explanation: The element is apparent ability to make or cause contact. Actual capacity is not required, and π need not prove fear — apprehension means expectation.
cards.why: Two traps in one fact pattern: actual ability and fear.

cards.scenario: A combat veteran, entirely unafraid, watches Δ swing a crowbar at his head and sidesteps it. Δ argues π was never frightened. What result?
options: No assault — apprehension requires fear
Assault — apprehension means expectation, and fear is not necessary
No assault — π avoided the blow
Assault, but damages are barred without fear
cards.explanation: Apprehension is expectation of the contact, not fear of it. π expected the contact, which is what the element requires; the absence of fear goes at most to damages.
cards.why: The word 'apprehension' invites the wrong reading — the outline defines it as expectation.

cards.scenario: Δ tells π, 'If you weren't my brother's friend, I would knock you flat right now,' standing still with folded arms. Can π establish a prima facie case for assault?
options: Yes — the threat was serious and Δ was plainly able to carry it out
Likely no — the contact apprehended must be imminent, and a threat framed on a condition contrary to fact communicates that no contact is coming
Yes — words alone can always constitute assault
No — words can never constitute assault
cards.explanation: The contact apprehended must be imminent. A statement conditioned on a state of affairs that does not exist tells π that no contact is coming now, so it does not produce expectation of imminent contact.
cards.why: TRICKY: (d) states an absolute that overshoots — the defect is imminence, not that words never suffice.

cards.scenario: Δ throws a rock at π intending to hit him. It misses, but π sees it coming and flinches. Which claim, and on what reasoning?
options: No claim — the rock missed
Assault — the intent to commit a battery supports a judgment for assault where the act intended to cause contact results instead in apprehension
Battery — intent is all that matters
IIED, since π was startled
cards.explanation: Where the act intended to cause contact results instead in apprehension, the intent to commit a battery will support a judgment for assault. π expected imminent contact, which completes the tort.
cards.why: Run the crossover whenever the intended result and the actual result diverge.

cards.text: A {{volitional}} act intended to cause plaintiff to be {{confined}} in a {{bounded}} space and which causes confinement with {{injury}} or {{awareness}}.
cards.why: Complete upon confinement of which π is aware, or which causes π harm.

cards.scenario: A store manager tells π, 'Stay right here or I will have your car towed and call your employer.' π stays two hours. No one touches her. Can π establish a prima facie case?
options: No — π was free to walk out and no one restrained her
Potentially yes — physical restraint is not necessary; a threat of harm to π, π's property, or another person may be enough to confine
No — threats to property are never confinement
Yes — automatically, because π remained
cards.explanation: Physical restraint is not necessary. Abuse of authority, or a threat of harm to π, π's property, or another person, might be enough to confine — the 'stay right here or I'll...' pattern.
cards.why: Threats to property and to third persons both count.

cards.scenario: π could leave a locked room through a window opening onto a third-story ledge. She stays. Was π confined within the meaning of the tort?
options: No — an escape route existed
Yes — the requirement is no apparent escape, or alternatively a risk of harm in escape; a route risking a fall does not defeat confinement
No — π consented by remaining
Yes — because any locked room is a bounded space
cards.explanation: The requirement is stated in the alternative: no apparent escape, or risk of harm in escaping. Either branch satisfies the element, and an escape that would require risking a fall is not one π must take.
cards.why: The disjunctive is easy to miss.

cards.scenario: Δ locks a storeroom at closing, unaware that π is inside. π is trapped overnight and is aware of it throughout. What result?
options: π establishes the prima facie case — the act was volitional and caused confinement with awareness
π cannot establish the prima facie case — the intent element requires intent to cause confinement, and Δ had none
π establishes it because intent is presumed from the locking
π cannot establish it because a storeroom is not a bounded space
cards.explanation: A volitional act alone is not enough; the element is intent to cause confinement, or knowledge of a substantial certainty that confinement will occur. Δ had neither, so the intentional tort fails — though negligence may lie.
cards.why: TRICKY: volitional act and intent are separate elements, and this pattern separates them.

cards.text: So outrageous in {{character}}, so extreme in {{degree}}, as to go beyond all possible bounds of {{decency}}, and to be regarded as {{atrocious}}, and utterly {{intolerable}} in a civilized society.
cards.why: The character and vulnerability of the victim is a factor in the determination.

cards.scenario: Which feature distinguishes IIED's mental state element from every other intentional tort studied?
options: It requires purpose only
It is satisfied by intentional OR reckless conduct
It requires knowledge to a substantial certainty
It requires no mental state at all
cards.explanation: IIED is the only tort in this set whose second element accepts recklessness as an alternative to intent. Every other intentional tort requires intent as defined by purpose or knowledge to a substantial certainty.
cards.why: TRICKY: an easy point to lose by reciting the general intent gate and stopping.

cards.scenario: Δ severely beats π's father in π's presence. Δ knew π was there and knew she was the victim's daughter. May π establish a prima facie case for IIED?
options: Never — π was not the target
Possibly — harm to a family member in π's presence might be sufficient if Δ knows π is present and related to the principal victim
Yes automatically — transferred intent supplies her claim
No — π must have been physically endangered herself
cards.explanation: Harm to a family member in the presence of π might be sufficient if Δ knows π is present and related to the principal victim. Note the conditions: presence, relationship, and Δ's knowledge of both.
cards.why: Without Δ's knowledge of presence and relationship, the bystander claim fails.

cards.scenario: π already suffers from an anxiety disorder. Δ's outrageous conduct makes it somewhat worse. What must π show on the severity element?
options: Nothing more — any worsening suffices
That the exacerbation caused by Δ was itself severe
That Δ knew of the pre-existing condition
That the condition was newly diagnosed
cards.explanation: Where π has a pre-existing condition, the exacerbation caused by Δ must be severe. The baseline distress does not count toward the element — only the increment Δ caused.
cards.why: TRICKY: the eggshell instinct pulls toward (a), but severity is measured on the exacerbation.

cards.scenario: Δ tells π, 'Pay by Friday or next week my associates will break both your legs.' No violence follows. Can the threat satisfy the outrageousness element?
options: No — only completed violence can be outrageous
Yes — threats of future physical violence to π or another might be sufficient
No — the threat was not imminent, so nothing is actionable
Yes — but only as assault
cards.explanation: Threats of future physical violence to π or another might be sufficient for IIED. Note the contrast with assault, where the apprehended contact must be imminent; IIED carries no imminence requirement.
cards.why: The absence of imminence defeats assault but not IIED — that contrast is the point.

cards.scenario: Δ walks across a field in the honest and reasonable belief that it is her own land. It is π's. Can π establish a prima facie case for trespass to land?
options: No — Δ lacked intent to trespass
Yes — only the act need be intended, not the tortious result; Δ intended to walk where she walked
No — unless π posted the boundary
Yes — but only if the land was damaged
cards.explanation: The volitional act element requires only that Δ be in control of the act and intend to act as she does. Only the act need be intended, not the tortious result. And since the interference is the injury, no harm to the land is required.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'I thought it was mine' feels like it should defeat intent — it does not.

cards.scenario: A factory floods π's yard with noise and odor around the clock. π pleads trespass to land. What result?
options: Trespass — the noise and odor physically enter the property
Not trespass — odor and noise are nuisance; trespass requires intrusion by a person or physical substance
Trespass — the interference is the injury
Not trespass — unless π proves damages
cards.explanation: Trespass requires intrusion by a person or by some physical substance. Odor and noise are nuisance; vibration is strict liability or nuisance. Classifying the intrusion is the first move.
cards.why: Three categories to keep straight: physical substance, vibration, and odor/noise.

cards.scenario: Δ crosses a corner of π's land leaving no trace and doing no damage. π sues. What result?
options: π cannot establish a prima facie case — no damages
π establishes the tort — the interference is the injury, and harm to the land is not necessary, though it would increase recoverable damages
π cannot establish it unless Δ was warned off
π establishes it only for emotional harm
cards.explanation: The interference is the injury. Harm to the land is not necessary to establish the tort, but if present it increases the damages recoverable. The tort is complete upon entry.
cards.why: Contrast trespass to chattels, where no dispossession, damage, or impairment means no tort at all.

cards.scenario: Δ borrows π's ladder without asking for an hour and returns it in perfect condition. π never needed it and never noticed. What result?
options: Trespass to chattels — any unpermitted use is an interference
No tort — no dispossession, damage, or impairment of use means no trespass to chattels
Trespass to chattels — the interference is the injury
Conversion, since Δ exercised dominion
cards.explanation: The dispossession, damage, or impairment constitutes the tort: no dispossession, damage, or impairment, no tort. Option (c) imports the trespass to land rule, which is precisely the distinction being tested.
cards.why: TRICKY: the 'interference is the injury' rule belongs to land, not chattels.

cards.scenario: Δ lets the air out of π's tires. They are undamaged and easily reinflated, but π misses a day of work. What result?
options: No tort — the chattel was neither taken nor damaged
Trespass to chattels — impairment of use is one of the three routes, and losses caused by impairment of use are recoverable
Conversion — π lost the use of the car
Trespass to chattels, but recovery is limited to the cost of reinflating
cards.explanation: Impairment of use is one of the three ways the interference element is satisfied, and damages include losses caused by impairment of use — here the lost day of work — alongside cost of repair and fair rental value.
cards.why: Impairment of use reaches harms where the chattel itself is untouched.

cards.scenario: Δ takes π's car and sells it to an untraceable buyer. What is the remedy, and what is it called?
options: Cost of repair; restitution
Payment of the full value of the chattel plus incidental losses — in effect a forced sale
Fair rental value for the period of dispossession
Nominal damages only
cards.explanation: Conversion by permanent dispossession warrants payment by Δ of the full value of the chattel to the rightful possessor — in effect a forced sale — with incidental losses also recoverable.
cards.why: The remedy defines the tort: full value marks conversion, not trespass to chattels.

cards.scenario: Δ keeps π's painting three days past the agreed return date, then returns it unharmed. π pleads conversion. What result?
options: Conversion — any unauthorized retention is conversion
Likely trespass to chattels rather than conversion — conversion requires permanent dispossession or substantial destruction warranting payment of full value
No tort at all, since the painting came back
Conversion, because paintings are unique
cards.explanation: Conversion requires permanent dispossession or substantial destruction, such as would warrant payment of the full value. A three-day delay falls far short; the interference sounds in trespass to chattels.
cards.why: The two chattel torts differ in degree, and equitable factors may be dispositive in close cases.

cards.scenario: Two Δs each keep π's identical tools for a month. One returns them; the other's are stolen from his shed and never recovered. Do both Δs commit the same tort?
options: Yes — both interfered for the same period
No — duration alone does not decide it; only the second produced a permanent dispossession warranting payment of full value
Yes — both are conversions because both exceeded a reasonable time
No — the second Δ has a defense because the theft was not his fault
cards.explanation: The line between trespass to chattels and conversion turns on the severity of the interference, and equitable factors might be dispositive in close cases. Identical durations can produce different torts where one ends in permanent dispossession.
cards.why: TRICKY: (d) invites a fault analysis that has no place in an intentional tort.

cards.scenario: A surgeon with consent to operate on the right ear finds the left is worse, operates on it in good faith, and the outcome is excellent. Does the affirmative defense of consent attach?
options: Yes — the good result cures any defect
No — the scope of consent may not be exceeded, and Δ's good faith or a good result will not cause a court to imply consent
Yes — consent to ear surgery covers both ears
No — but only because the surgeon failed to wake the patient and ask
cards.explanation: Two rules converge: the scope of consent may not be exceeded, and Δ's good faith or a good result will not be a basis for a court to imply consent.
cards.why: Both halves matter — scope and the refusal to imply consent from good outcomes.

cards.scenario: A hockey player is struck in the back of the head well after the whistle. Δ pleads consent to the violence of the sport. What result?
options: Consent bars the claim — hockey is a violent sport
Consent covers conduct within the customs of the sport, which may extend beyond the written rules, but does not reach a deliberate strike after play has ended
Consent bars the claim because π signed a waiver
Consent never applies to athletes
cards.explanation: Consent is limited to contact or otherwise tortious activity within the customs of the sport or activity, and this may go beyond the rules of the game. Custom, not the rulebook, marks the boundary — and a blow after the whistle falls outside it.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'may go beyond the rules' cuts both ways — broader than the rules, still bounded by custom.

cards.scenario: π stands in a vaccination line, watches others, and holds out her arm to the nurse without speaking. Which form of consent is presented?
options: Express, because the gesture was deliberate
Apparent — a gesture or behavior indicating consent as it would be understood by a reasonable person under all the circumstances, including in some cases silence
Implied, since the court supplies it from the nature of the activity
None, since π said nothing
cards.explanation: Apparent consent is a gesture or behavior by π communicating or otherwise indicating consent, as a reasonable person would understand it under all the circumstances, including in some cases π's silence. Express consent requires a clear expression, spoken or written.
cards.why: Apparent and implied often overlap; the tell is whether π acted, or the court inferred from the activity.

cards.scenario: Δ conceals a communicable disease he has a duty to disclose and obtains π's agreement to contact. What is the legal effect on the consent given?
options: Valid — π agreed to the contact that occurred
Invalid — consent obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence where there is a duty to disclose is vitiated by failure to disclose information material to the consent
Valid unless π asked and Δ lied
Invalid only if π contracts the disease
cards.explanation: Consent is invalid if obtained by deceit, misrepresentation, or silence concerning a matter as to which there is a duty to disclose, and is vitiated by failure to disclose information material to the consent. Silence is expressly included.
cards.why: Silence vitiates as readily as an affirmative lie where a duty to disclose exists.

cards.scenario: Δ reasonably but wrongly believes π is reaching for a weapon, and shoves him. π was reaching for a dropped phone. Does the privilege attach?
options: No — Δ was mistaken about the threat
Yes — the privilege is present where Δ reasonably believes force is necessary, even if Δ is mistaken
No — unless π appeared armed to a bystander as well
Yes — but only if Δ apologizes
cards.explanation: The privilege turns on reasonable belief and is expressly available even where Δ is mistaken. Reasonableness, not accuracy, is the test.
cards.why: Contrast defense of others, where courts divide on mistake — though Franklin protects the good-faith intervenor.

cards.scenario: Δ knocks his attacker down, ending the threat, then kicks him twice more. Does the privilege attach to the kicks?
options: Yes — Δ was attacked first
No — there is no privilege to retaliate, and only such force as is necessary in the circumstances is privileged
Yes — doubts are resolved in favor of Δ
No — Δ was required to retreat before using any force
cards.explanation: There is no privilege to retaliate, and only necessary force is privileged. When the threat ended, so did the privilege.
cards.why: Self-defense is forward-looking; retaliation is a different thing entirely.

cards.scenario: π subjects Δ to a stream of racial and personal abuse. Δ punches him. Does the privilege of self-defense attach?
options: Yes — the abuse was outrageous
No — insults, however vile, never create a privilege to use force; it is not self-defense at common law
Yes — words can constitute a threat of battery
No — but the abuse reduces π's damages
cards.explanation: Insults, 'disses,' and vituperations, no matter how vile, do not create a privilege to use force. The rule is categorical.
cards.why: TRICKY: the abuse may support Δ's IIED claim; it never licenses the punch.

cards.scenario: Δ is threatened in her own kitchen and could safely leave through the back door. She stands her ground and uses force. Does the privilege attach?
options: No — retreat is required in Franklin and she could have retreated safely
Yes — retreat is never required inside one's own home, even in a retreat jurisdiction
No — the common law required retreat everywhere without exception
Yes — because Franklin has abolished the retreat requirement
cards.explanation: Retreat is required in Franklin and at common law, but never inside one's own home. The home exception is what saves Δ here.
cards.why: Know both halves: Franklin IS a retreat jurisdiction, and the home is the exception.

cards.scenario: A bystander in Franklin intervenes with force to protect a man he reasonably believes is being beaten. The man was in fact the aggressor. Does the privilege attach?
options: No — the privilege is derivative, and the aggressor had none to derive
Yes in Franklin — the intervenor's privilege is present even when mistaken as to the attack, provided he acted in good faith
Yes in every jurisdiction — mistake never defeats the privilege
No — defense of others requires a family relationship
cards.explanation: Courts are divided on mistake, but the rule in the State of Franklin is that the intervenor's privilege is present even when mistaken as to the attack on the other, provided the intervenor acted in good faith.
cards.why: TRICKY: the general derivative rule points the other way — Franklin's rule is the one that governs your exam.

cards.scenario: An intervenor uses substantially more force than the person defended could lawfully have used. Does the privilege attach to the excess?
options: Yes — intervenors are given latitude for split-second judgment
No — the intervenor's conduct is governed by all the same rules that govern the victim's conduct in self-defense, including that only necessary force is privileged
Yes — if he acted in good faith
No — because only the victim may ever defend himself
cards.explanation: The privilege is derivative, so the intervenor is governed by all the same rules that govern the victim in self-defense. Good faith protects against a mistake about the attack in Franklin; it does not license excessive force.
cards.why: Derivative means it inherits the limits along with the privilege.

cards.scenario: Δ rigs a spring gun in a boarded-up, unoccupied farmhouse. It shoots a trespasser in the leg. Does the privilege attach?
options: Yes — he was preventing a tort against his property
No — deadly force may never be used to protect property alone, and one may not use a mechanical device to do what one could not do oneself
Yes — because he posted warning signs
No — but only because the trespasser was unarmed
cards.explanation: Both rules apply: deadly force may not be used to protect property, and a mechanical device may not do what Δ could not do in person. The house was unoccupied, so the Castle Doctrine framework does not enter.
cards.why: The mechanical-device rule stops Δ from evading the deadly force limit by automation.

cards.scenario: Δ shoves a postal carrier off the porch for entering the yard. Does the privilege attach?
options: Yes — it is Δ's property
No — there is no privilege to use force where the intrusion onto the property is lawful
Yes — provided the force was non-deadly
No — unless Δ first asked him to leave
cards.explanation: There is no privilege to use force where the intrusion is lawful. The meter reader and the postal carrier are the stock examples; the privilege presupposes a tort against the property, and a lawful entry is not one.
cards.why: Check the lawfulness of the entry before reaching the force question.

cards.scenario: An intruder breaks into Δ's home at night while the family sleeps inside. Which framework governs Δ's use of force?
options: Defense of property, so deadly force is categorically barred
A different framework — unlawful entry into an occupied home is treated as a threat to the occupiers, conceptually different and governed by different rules, with the Castle Doctrine applying
Defense of others only
Public necessity
cards.explanation: Unlawful entry into an occupied home is treated as a threat to the occupiers. It is conceptually different from defense of property and governed by different rules; the Castle Doctrine applies there.
cards.why: TRICKY: the bar on deadly force protects property, not occupants of an occupied home.

cards.scenario: A merchant with reasonable suspicion detains a customer in a back office for five hours without further inquiry. Does the privilege attach throughout?
options: Yes — reasonable suspicion existed at the outset
No as to the duration — the privilege permits detention only for a reasonable time to investigate
Yes — because no force was used
No — the privilege does not exist at common law
cards.explanation: Each component carries its own reasonableness limit: reasonable suspicion, reasonable force, on the premises, for a reasonable time to investigate. Suspicion opens the door but does not license indefinite detention.
cards.why: Take the components one at a time — a privilege can attach and then lapse.

cards.scenario: Who decides whether the merchant's suspicion, force, and detention time were reasonable?
options: The jury alone
The court in the first instance, then the jury
The court alone, as a matter of law
The merchant, subject to later review
cards.explanation: The determination of what is reasonable is for the court in the first instance, then for the jury. The court screens; the jury decides what survives the screen.
cards.why: Stated expressly — an easy point if you have it.

cards.scenario: Officials demolish π's house to create a firebreak, saving the town. What result at common law?
options: π recovers the full value of the house
No compensation is required at common law, though many states now provide for it by statute
π recovers the value of the land only
π recovers the house plus punitive damages
cards.explanation: Public necessity requires no compensation at common law; the rationale may have been that this particular property would have been destroyed anyway. Many states have since provided compensation by statute.
cards.why: Public necessity is complete; the contrast with private necessity is the payment.

cards.scenario: A fire officer destroys a shed he reasonably believes will carry flames to a school. The shed turns out to have been fireproof. Does the defense attach?
options: No — the destruction was in fact unnecessary
Yes — conduct is privileged where necessary, OR APPARENTLY NECESSARY, to prevent greater harm to the community
No — unless the school actually caught fire
Yes — but compensation is owed because he was mistaken
cards.explanation: The rule reaches conduct necessary or apparently necessary to prevent greater harm to the community, and no compensation is required at common law.
cards.why: TRICKY: hindsight makes the destruction look gratuitous; the standard is apparent necessity at the time.

cards.scenario: A ship moors to π's dock in a storm to save the vessel and crew, damaging the dock. What must Δ pay?
options: Nothing — necessity is a complete defense
The value of the damage to the dock, but no punitive damages and no nominal damages
The value of the dock plus punitive damages
Nothing, because π could not have compelled him to leave
cards.explanation: Private necessity is a defense, so no legal wrong is committed and the owner may not compel the user to desist, and there are no nominal damages. But the user must pay the value of any damage to the property, without punitive damages.
cards.why: Three damages rules in one: no nominal, yes actual, no punitive.

cards.scenario: During the storm, π unties the ship's lines and casts it off. The ship is wrecked. Is π subject to liability?
options: No — it is π's dock and he may exclude anyone
Yes — if the owner forces the user to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is liable
No — unless π acted maliciously
Yes — but only for the value of the mooring
cards.explanation: Because no legal wrong is committed by the privileged user, the owner may not compel him to desist; and if the owner does force him to desist and harm results to the user or the user's property, the owner is liable.
cards.why: This is what makes the privilege meaningful rather than merely a damages rule.

cards.scenario: Which statement correctly distinguishes public from private necessity?
options: Public necessity requires compensation; private necessity does not
Public necessity requires no compensation at common law; private necessity requires the user to pay the value of any damage to the property
Both require payment of actual damages
Neither is available against trespass to land
cards.explanation: Public necessity requires no compensation at common law, though many states now provide it by statute. Private necessity bars nominal and punitive damages but requires the user to pay the value of any damage done.
cards.why: TRICKY: the two run in opposite directions on compensation, and (a) reverses them.

cards.scenario: Δ's conduct fits no named privilege, but the circumstances were extraordinary and the response measured. Is any affirmative defense available?
options: No — the privileges are a closed list
Possibly justification — a catch-all recognizing that a privilege may arise in circumstances unanticipated before
Only public necessity
Only consent, if implied
cards.explanation: Justification is a catch-all: a privilege to commit an act otherwise tortious may arise in circumstances unanticipated before. The test is a measure of necessity under those particular circumstances, and the categories of privilege are not carved in stone.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'necessity' appears in the test, but this is the concept, not the necessity defense.

cards.scenario: π cracks a tooth on a shell fragment in a bowl of clam chowder. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: π recovers — any foreign material in food is contamination
π cannot establish this claim — contamination is not applied to harm caused by bones and stones natural to the food
π recovers only if the restaurant was negligent in straining the chowder
π recovers because the restaurant is in the business of selling food
cards.explanation: Contamination means poison, putrefaction, or foreign objects in food, and the doctrine is not applied to harm caused by bones and stones natural to the food. A shell in a shellfish dish is the paradigm. Negligence may still lie — say so.
cards.why: Pivot to negligence when strict liability fails on a limitation.

cards.scenario: A sealed jar leaves the factory clean. A stocker punctures the seal and mold develops. π sues the manufacturer. What result?
options: The manufacturer is subject to liability — it made the product that injured π
The manufacturer is not subject to liability — the product did not reach π in substantially the same condition as when it left its control
The manufacturer is subject to liability because mold is putrefaction
The manufacturer is subject to liability unless it proves the stocker acted intentionally
cards.explanation: The third element requires the product to reach the π-consumer in substantially the same condition as when it left the manufacturer's or seller's control. An intervening puncture breaks that chain as to the manufacturer.
cards.why: Element three resolves post-sale tampering and mishandling.

cards.scenario: A neighbor bakes π a pie as a gift. It contains a glass shard and π is injured. Can π establish a prima facie case in strict liability?
options: Yes — glass is a foreign object and it caused injury
No — Δ was not engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food product
Yes — the pie reached π in the same condition
No — gifts cannot give rise to tort liability
cards.explanation: The first element requires that Δ be engaged in the business of manufacturing or selling the food at issue. A casual gift-giver is not, so strict liability does not lie — though negligence might.
cards.why: Element one screens out the non-commercial Δ before contamination is ever reached.

cards.text: A wild animal is an animal that is not by {{custom}} devoted to the {{service}} of {{mankind}} at the {{time}} and in the {{place}} in which it is kept.
cards.why: The definition is relative to time and place — an animal domesticated in one society may be wild in another.

cards.scenario: Δ keeps a tiger in a reinforced enclosure and takes every conceivable precaution. A vandal cuts the gate and the tiger mauls π. Is Δ subject to liability?
options: No — the precautions establish reasonable care
Yes — Δ is held to the knowledge of the dangers arising from wildness, scienter is presumed, and liability attaches without fault
No — the vandal's act breaks the chain
Yes — but only if this tiger had attacked before
cards.explanation: For wild animals, Δ is held to the knowledge of the dangers arising from the animal's wildness and scienter is presumed. Liability is without fault, so precautions do not answer the prima facie case.
cards.why: Presumed scienter is the defining feature of the wild-animal track.

cards.scenario: A zoo elephant, startled by thunder, sits on π's foot while being led to its pen. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: Strict liability — an elephant is a wild animal and it caused harm
Strict liability likely does not lie — the harm flowed from the animal's size, not from a dangerous propensity arising from its wildness; negligence might lie
Strict liability — scienter is presumed
Strict liability — unless the zoo proves the thunder was unforeseeable
cards.explanation: The caveat: if the harm was caused by some other characteristic of the animal, other than its wildness, strict liability will not lie, but another cause of action, such as negligence, might. Crushing weight is not a vicious propensity arising from wildness.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'wild animal' plus 'harm' is not the test — the harm must flow from the wildness.

cards.scenario: A trapper sells a captured wolf to a roadside attraction, which keeps it a year before it bites π. π sues the trapper. What result?
options: The trapper is subject to liability — he captured and first harbored the wolf
The trapper is not subject to liability — Δ must have been the last to have kept or harbored the animal
Both are subject to liability jointly
The trapper is subject to liability because scienter is presumed as to wolves
cards.explanation: The element requires that Δ owned, kept, or harbored the animal, and Δ must have been the last to have kept or harbored it. Having passed the wolf on a year earlier, the trapper falls outside the rule.
cards.why: The 'last to keep or harbor' gloss decides which of several possessors answers.

cards.scenario: A placid dog with no history bites π for the first time. Its owner had no reason to suspect danger. Can π establish a prima facie case?
options: Yes — dog owners are strictly liable at common law
No — scienter is not presumed for domestic animals, and Δ had neither actual nor constructive knowledge of abnormal dangerousness
Yes — biting is inherently abnormally dangerous behavior
No — because π approached the dog
cards.explanation: Unlike wild animals, scienter is not presumed for domestic animals. π must show actual or constructive knowledge of the abnormal dangerousness, which usually arises from previous attacks or risk-creating behavior.
cards.why: This is the single most testable contrast between the two animal tracks.

cards.scenario: A dog has lunged and snapped at three delivery drivers in six months, restrained each time, never making contact. It then bites π. What is the owner's strongest argument?
options: No scienter — the dog had never actually bitten anyone
The argument fails: abnormal dangerousness usually arises from previous attacks OR other behavior that creates risk of harm, and repeated lunging supplies at least constructive knowledge
π assumed the risk by approaching
Domestic animals can never support strict liability
cards.explanation: Abnormal dangerousness usually arises from previous attacks on people or other animals, or other behavior that creates a risk of harm. Prior contact is not required, and repeated lunging supplies constructive knowledge.
cards.why: TRICKY: the 'one free bite' intuition overreads the rule — risk-creating behavior counts.

cards.scenario: Δ watches his brother's dog for a week, knowing it has bitten twice. It bites π. Δ argues he does not own the dog. What result?
options: Not subject to liability — the element requires ownership
Subject to liability — the element is satisfied by one who kept, possessed, or harbored the animal, and need not own it
Not subject to liability — scienter belongs to the brother
Subject to liability only if he was negligent in restraining it
cards.explanation: The first element is satisfied by one who kept, possessed, or harbored the animal, and expressly need not own it. Δ knew of the prior bites, so scienter is established as to him.
cards.why: Possession plus knowledge is enough; title is beside the point.

cards.text: One who carries on an {{abnormally}} {{dangerous}} activity is subject to liability for harm to the person, land, or chattels of another resulting from the activity, although he has exercised the {{utmost}} {{care}} to prevent the harm. This strict liability is limited to the {{kind}} of {{harm}}, the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous.
cards.why: § 519(2) is the scope limitation — the reason harm outside the characteristic risk is not covered.

cards.prompt: Name the § 520 factors. Which is the single most important, and which must you be able to reproduce?
answer: These are FACTORS, NOT elements of a cause of action — say this.
(a) Existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land or chattels of others;
(b) Likelihood that the harm that results from it will be great — likelihood does NOT mean probability;
(c) INABILITY TO ELIMINATE THE RISK BY THE EXERCISE OF REASONABLE CARE — THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FACTOR;
(d) Extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage;
(e) Inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on;
(f) Extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
You need to be able to reproduce (a), (b), and (c). The whole list is not required.
cards.fallback: A high degree of {{risk}}; likelihood the harm will be {{great}}; inability to {{eliminate}} the risk by the exercise of reasonable care; the extent to which the activity is not a matter of {{common}} usage; {{inappropriateness}} to the place where carried on; and the extent to which its {{value}} to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes.
cards.why: Lead with (c) — it is the most important factor and the reason the activity gets strict liability at all.

cards.scenario: Δ blasts lawfully. A mile away, π's mink are alarmed by the noise and kill their own kits. Which statement best analyzes the claim?
options: π recovers — blasting is ultrahazardous and the harm resulted from it

π cannot recover on this theory — § 519(2) limits strict liability to the kind of harm the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous, and nervous mink are outside concussion, vibration, and flying debris
π recovers — all the § 520 factors favor π
π cannot recover — mink are not property
cards.explanation: Section 519(2) limits strict liability to the kind of harm the possibility of which makes the activity abnormally dangerous. For blasting those risks are concussion of air, vibration of ground, and flying debris — not the reaction of animals at a distance.
cards.why: TRICKY: causation alone is not enough; the scope limitation in § 519(2) is the trap.

cards.scenario: Δ argues its activity cannot be abnormally dangerous because only three of the § 520 considerations point that way. What is the strongest response?
options: Δ is correct — a majority must be satisfied
Δ is incorrect — these are factors to be considered, not elements of a cause of action, and no fixed number must be met
Δ is correct — all must be satisfied
Δ is incorrect — only the first factor matters
cards.explanation: Section 520 says the listed considerations are factors to be weighed, and the outline flags expressly that they are not elements of a cause of action. Say so in your answer.
cards.why: The factors-not-elements point is one the professor wants stated out loud.

cards.scenario: Under § 520, what does 'likelihood that the harm that results will be great' ask?
options: The statistical probability that harm will occur
Not probability — it asks about the magnitude of the harm if it does occur
The frequency with which the activity is conducted
The chance Δ will be sued
cards.explanation: The outline flags this specifically: likelihood does not mean probability. The first factor already addresses the degree of risk; this one asks how great the harm will be should it materialize.
cards.why: TRICKY: the ordinary meaning of 'likelihood' points the wrong way.

cards.scenario: Δ proves it followed every industry protocol and executed the shot perfectly. Debris still damages π's home. What is the legal effect of that showing on the prima facie case?
options: It defeats liability — reasonable care is a defense
None — § 519 imposes liability although Δ exercised the utmost care to prevent the harm
It reduces damages proportionally
It shifts the burden to π to prove negligence
cards.explanation: Section 519 states that liability attaches although the actor has exercised the utmost care to prevent the harm. That is the whole content of liability without fault.
cards.why: Quote the 'utmost care' language — it is the sentence that answers the care argument.

cards.scenario: π climbs over a warning barrier to photograph a bear and is clawed. On what affirmative defense should the zoo rely?
options: Contributory negligence
Voluntary assumption of a known risk — the only complete defense to strict liability at common law
Comparative fault
Consent to the animal's wildness
cards.explanation: At common law only voluntary assumption of a known risk is a complete defense to claims for strict liability. Deliberately crossing a barrier to approach a bear is the paradigm case.
cards.why: One defense — do not import negligence defenses into a strict liability answer.

cards.scenario: π is inattentive and walks past blasting warning signs he never reads, and is struck by debris. Δ pleads contributory negligence. What result under the common law rule applied in this course?
options: Complete bar — contributory negligence bars any tort claim
Not the operative defense — the only complete defense is voluntary assumption of a KNOWN risk, and inattention is neither voluntary acceptance nor knowledge
Damages reduced by π's share of fault
Complete bar because π entered the area voluntarily
cards.explanation: The defense is voluntary assumption of a known risk. Carelessness falling short of knowing acceptance does not fit it, and ordinary contributory negligence is not the defense identified for strict liability in this course.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'voluntary' and 'known' both do work — inattention satisfies neither.

cards.concept: The general duty — state it verbatim
cards.text: A legal {{obligation}} to act as an {{ordinary}}, {{reasonable}}, {{prudent}} person under all the {{circumstances}}.
cards.why: The outline says this must be part of your answer. Write it before you narrow to the specific content.

cards.scenario: What must every negligence answer contain before the specific content of the duty is discussed?
options: A citation to a governing case
The general duty: a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances
The Hand formula calculation
A statement of the burden of proof
cards.explanation: The general duty is a legal obligation to act as an ordinary, reasonable, prudent person under all the circumstances, and the outline states it must be part of your answer. Then name a source for the specific content — do not leave duty generic.
cards.why: Two moves: state the general duty, then name the source of the specific content.

cards.scenario: Δ has a significantly below-average IQ and fails to appreciate an obvious risk. What standard of care governs Δ's conduct?
options: A reasonable person of similar intelligence
The ordinary, reasonable person — low IQ receives no allowance
A subjective standard based on Δ's actual capacities
The child standard, by analogy
cards.explanation: Among the mental caveats, low IQ receives no allowance: the duty remains that of an ordinary, reasonable person. Contrast physical limitations, which are accounted for.
cards.why: Physical limitations are accommodated; mental ones generally are not.

cards.scenario: A blind pedestrian collides with π after failing to notice a hazard visible only to sighted people. What standard of care governs?
options: The ordinary reasonable sighted person
The duty of a reasonable blind person to others
A subjective standard based on Δ's own habits
Strict liability
cards.explanation: Physical limitations are accounted for: the outline frames it as the duty of a reasonable blind or deaf person, or a reasonable wheelchair-bound person, to others.
cards.why: The contrast with low IQ and insanity is the point of the list.

cards.scenario: An off-duty chemist recognizes a hazard a layperson would miss and says nothing. What standard of care governs?
options: The ordinary reasonable person, who would not have known
Δ must use his superior knowledge
The professional standard, but only if he was on duty
A subjective standard of Δ's choosing
cards.explanation: Superior knowledge is the one caveat that raises the bar: a person with superior knowledge must use that knowledge. It is the mirror image of 'lacking knowledge,' which gets no allowance downward.
cards.why: TRICKY: (c) invites you to require a professional setting, which the caveat does not.

cards.scenario: A twelve-year-old handles a rifle carelessly and shoots π. What standard of care governs?
options: A reasonably prudent child of like age, education, intelligence, and experience
The adult standard — a gun is the adult standard
A subjective standard based on this child's maturity
Strict liability
cards.explanation: When conducting dangerous activities generally reserved for adults, children are held to an adult standard. There is no clear rule, and the hint is to look at the thing the child is using — but a gun is the adult standard.
cards.why: The gun rule is the one bright line in an otherwise fuzzy area.

cards.scenario: A child Δ argues the standard should account for his own unusual immaturity compared to others his age. What result?
options: Accepted — the standard is subjective as to children
Rejected — the standard is objective: based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child, but not on this particular child
Accepted if supported by expert testimony
Rejected — children are always held to the adult standard
cards.explanation: The child standard is objective. It is a general standard based on children with characteristics similar to those of this child — like age, education, intelligence, and experience — but it is not based on this particular child.
cards.why: TRICKY: the list of characteristics sounds individualized, but the outline stresses it remains objective.

cards.scenario: A ten-year-old on a bicycle collides with π. What standard of care governs?
options: Adult — bicycles are vehicles
The child standard — a bicycle sits with small toys and a ball, not with a tractor, snowmobile, or gun
Adult — any activity causing injury triggers the adult standard
Strict liability
cards.explanation: There is no clear rule for which activities are generally reserved for adults. The hint is to look at the thing the child is using: tractor, snowmobile, and gun on one side; small toys, ball, and bicycle on the other.
cards.why: The comparison list is the closest thing to guidance the outline gives.

cards.scenario: Δ proves it complied with every custom of its industry. What is the legal effect of that showing?
options: Complete defense — compliance with custom establishes due care
Important evidence that courts ordinarily follow, but it does not bind the court or jury and may be challenged on Hand Formula considerations
Irrelevant — custom is inadmissible
Conclusive only if the custom is written
cards.explanation: Custom is the duty an industry imposes on itself, admissible through expert testimony. It does not bind the court or jury but is important evidence, and courts ordinarily follow it — subject to challenge on Hand Formula grounds.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'courts ordinarily follow it' tempts you to treat custom as conclusive.

cards.scenario: How is evidence of an industry custom admitted?
options: By judicial notice
Through expert testimony
By stipulation only
It is not admissible
cards.explanation: Custom of an industry or trade and the standards of a profession are admissible in evidence through expert testimony.
cards.why: A small point, easy to state, and stated expressly in the outline.

cards.prompt: Name the five excuses for a statutory violation under § 288A.
answer: (a) Reasonable because of the actor's INCAPACITY
(b) He neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance
(c) Unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply
(d) Confronted by an EMERGENCY not due to his own misconduct
(e) COMPLIANCE WOULD INVOLVE A GREATER RISK OF HARM to the actor or to others — the MOST IMPORTANT excuse
The excuse may, but need not, be built into the statute itself.
cards.fallback: Reasonable because of {{incapacity}}; neither {{knows}} nor should know of the occasion for compliance; {{unable}} after reasonable diligence to comply; confronted by an {{emergency}} not due to his own misconduct; compliance would involve a greater {{risk}} of harm.
cards.why: The outline flags (e) as the most important excuse.

cards.scenario: A statute requires fencing livestock to keep animals off highways. Δ's unfenced sheep contract disease from a neighbor's herd. Does negligence per se apply?
options: Yes — the statute was violated and harm followed
No — the statute must protect against injury of the type suffered, and disease is not the highway-collision harm it targets
Yes — π is within the protected class
No — because the statute did not mention disease
cards.explanation: Both prongs are required: a class of persons including π, and injury of the type suffered by π. Failing the type-of-injury prong, negligence per se cannot be applied.
cards.why: Most negligence per se questions are decided on the two-prong screen.

cards.scenario: Negligence per se cannot be applied because only one prong is met. What happens to π's case?
options: It is dismissed
Treat the cause of action as common law negligence; the statute may still be a useful source of ideas for the content of duty but need not be adopted per se
It converts to strict liability
The jury must disregard the statute entirely
cards.explanation: If a statute applies to only one of the two requirements, negligence per se cannot be applied. In such a case, treat the cause of action as common law negligence; the statute might still be useful as a source of ideas for the content of duty, but need not be adopted per se by the court. Breach, cause in fact, and proximate cause are applied as they ordinarily would be.
cards.why: Failing negligence per se is not failing the case — say so and continue.

cards.scenario: Δ crosses a double yellow line, violating a traffic statute, to avoid a child who darted into the road. Sued by an oncoming motorist. What is Δ's strongest argument?
options: No violation occurred
The violation is excused: compliance would have involved a greater risk of harm — the most important excuse under § 288A
The statute does not protect motorists
Negligence per se never applies to traffic statutes
cards.explanation: Even where both prongs are met, negligence per se may be inapplicable because an excuse applies. The excuse may, but need not, be built into the statute, or may be adopted from § 288A — and the most important is that compliance would involve a greater risk of harm to the actor or others.
cards.why: Run the excuse check after the two-prong test, not instead of it.

cards.scenario: Negligence per se applies and no excuse is available. What has π established?
options: The entire prima facie case
Duty and breach — the jury is bound on those; cause in fact must still be separately proven, and proximate cause remains an element though rarely contested
Duty only
Liability, subject only to proof of damages
cards.explanation: If applicable, negligence per se binds the jury on duty and breach. The violation must also be a cause in fact of the harm, and a proximate cause — though proximate cause is rarely an issue because by the nature of negligence per se π is a foreseeable π suffering foreseeable harm.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'per se' sounds total; it decides two elements and leaves causation to π.

cards.scenario: Why is proximate cause rarely contested where negligence per se applies?
options: Statutes eliminate the requirement
Because by the nature of negligence per se, π is a foreseeable π suffering foreseeable harm
Because the jury is bound on all elements
Because cause in fact subsumes it
cards.explanation: Proximate cause is rarely an issue because by the nature of negligence per se the plaintiff is a foreseeable plaintiff suffering foreseeable harm — which is exactly what the two prongs establish.
cards.why: The two prongs do double duty: they screen entry and resolve foreseeability.

cards.scenario: A rural physician argues he should be measured against other physicians in his small town. What result?
options: Correct — the locality rule governs
Incorrect — for physicians the standard of care is national; the old locality rule is out in Franklin
Correct if no specialists practice nearby
Incorrect only as to specialists
cards.explanation: For physicians the standard of care is national. The outline states flatly that the old locality rule is out in Franklin.
cards.why: A clean rule with no qualifiers — free points if you have it.

cards.scenario: π's expert on the professional standard has never reviewed the record in this case. Is there a defect in π's position?
options: No — familiarity with the standard is enough
Yes — the expert must be familiar with the professional standard of care AND with the case before the court
No — expert testimony is never required
Yes — but only in medical cases
cards.explanation: Expert testimony is generally necessary for the professional standard, and the expert must be familiar with the professional standard of care and with the case before the court. Both are required.
cards.why: TRICKY: the second half of the requirement is easy to omit.

cards.scenario: A surgeon performs a procedure flawlessly within the standard of care but never disclosed a known risk of nerve damage, which materializes. On what theory does π's claim proceed?
options: Battery, since π did not consent to nerve damage
Negligence — informed consent is part of the physician's duty and standard of care, and failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery
Strict liability
No claim — the treatment met the standard of care
cards.explanation: Informed consent is part of the physician's duty and standard of care, and failure to inform is handled as negligence, not battery, in Franklin and generally in the US. It is precisely the theory used where treatment was properly performed but an adverse outcome followed.
cards.why: TRICKY: unconsented touching sounds like battery, but the doctrine is deliberately framed in negligence.

cards.scenario: By what measure is the materiality of a risk judged in Franklin?
options: What a reasonable physician would disclose
Those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient
What this particular patient says she would have wanted to know
Whatever the hospital's consent form lists
cards.explanation: The duty is to inform of facts and risks material to the patient's decision, measured in Franklin by those facts that would be material to a reasonable patient in the same situation as the plaintiff-patient.
cards.why: Reasonable-patient, not reasonable-physician, and not this particular patient.

cards.scenario: A driver suffers a seizure, crashes through an unbarricaded roadside work zone, and injures π, a worker. The general contractor argues the driver caused the harm. Did the contractor owe π a duty?
options: No — the driver's negligence was an intervening cause
Yes — the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor can become the basis of a duty imposed on another; negligent driving is foreseeable at a roadside site
No — contractors owe duties only to their own employees
Yes — but only if the contractor knew this driver was ill
cards.explanation: Sometimes the foreseeable negligence of one tortfeasor becomes the basis of a duty imposed on another. The general contractor had a duty to erect barriers protecting workers at a roadside site precisely because negligent driving is foreseeable.
cards.why: The foreseeability of the other party's negligence creates the duty rather than excusing it.

cards.scenario: The facts fit no statute, custom, or precedent. What is the method for identifying a possible duty?
options: Conclude there is no duty
Reverse engineer: review the sequence from Δ's conduct to π's harm, determine what Δ could have done differently to prevent or minimize it, and treat that conduct as the possible duty
Apply strict liability
Ask whether Δ acted in good faith
cards.explanation: Review the sequence of facts leading from Δ's conduct to π's harm and determine what Δ could have done differently. Whatever conduct, to do or to refrain from, would have prevented the harm is the conduct considered as a possible duty — and its cost is the cost of avoidance under Hand.
cards.why: The method feeds directly into the Hand formula's second variable.

cards.scenario: From what vantage point is the Hand analysis conducted?
options: With hindsight, knowing the harm that occurred
Metaphorically at the place where, and the time just before, the conduct took place
At the time of trial
From π's perspective at the moment of injury
cards.explanation: We put ourselves metaphorically at the place where, and at the time just before, the conduct took place, and consider likelihood and severity as we would have understood them then.
cards.why: Ex ante, not ex post. No hindsight.

cards.scenario: Which two considerations together constitute THE RISK?
options: Cost to Δ and social cost
The likelihood that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur
Foreseeability and proximate cause
Industry custom and the applicable statute
cards.explanation: The likelihood, as we would have understood it then, that some harm would occur, and the likely severity of that harm should it occur — these together are the risk. The cost of avoidance sits on the other side of the comparison.
cards.why: State the pairing explicitly in your answer; the outline names it.

cards.scenario: π shows real risk and a precisely quantified, modest cost of avoidance. Must the court impose a duty?
options: Yes — where cost is less than risk, duty follows
Not necessarily — this is not arithmetic but social policy, comparing incommensurables, and even with risk and a measurable cost of avoidance there might still be no duty
Yes — Hand's formula is a mathematical test
No — cost of avoidance is irrelevant to duty
cards.explanation: The comparison is not arithmetic; it is social policy, and it unavoidably requires comparing incommensurables. Even where there is risk and a reasonably measurable cost of avoidance, there might still be no duty.
cards.why: TRICKY: the B<PL formulation invites arithmetic, which the outline expressly disclaims. Say 'this is social policy, not math.'

cards.scenario: An entire profession declines to require a cheap, safe screening test. π is harmed by the undetected condition. How can Hand be used?
options: It cannot — custom sets the standard
Offensively — Hand can be used to attack a custom or professional standard as an inadequate duty in light of the risk, and a court may impose the duty as a matter of law
Only to defend Δ
Only where a statute applies
cards.explanation: Hand's formula can be used to attack a custom of an industry or a professional standard as an inadequate duty in light of the risk. In Helling — small likelihood, very high severity, vanishingly low cost of avoidance — the court imposed the duty as a matter of law despite the profession's contrary standard.
cards.why: This is why custom is important evidence rather than a safe harbor.

cards.scenario: Whose costs are weighed on the avoidance side?
options: Only this Δ's out-of-pocket cost
The cost to this Δ, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty
Only π's cost of self-protection
Only costs capable of precise measurement
cards.explanation: We consider the cost, including the cost to this Δ, the cost to others similarly situated, and the social costs, if any, of imposing the duty. This is social policy, not math.
cards.why: Imposing a duty binds a whole class of actors, not just this Δ.

cards.scenario: Δ negligently breaks π's arm. π has a rare condition and the break causes permanent disability far beyond what anyone would expect. Extent of liability?
options: Liable only for the ordinary consequences of a broken arm
Liable in full — the eggshell plaintiff rule: the harm is the same general type as foreseeable but more severe, and Δ remains liable
Not liable, since the severity was unforeseeable
Liable only if Δ knew of the condition
cards.explanation: Eggshell plaintiff: where the harm that results is of the same general type as foreseeable but more severe than foreseeable, Δ is still liable.
cards.why: Same TYPE, greater SEVERITY — that is the eggshell pattern.

cards.scenario: π suffers a physical injury and also develops severe, unusually acute psychological harm. What is Δ's exposure for the psychological harm?
options: None — psychological harm requires a separate duty
Full — psychological harm is always foreseeable when π suffers physical harm, and Δ is liable for all of it even if unforeseeably severe
Limited to what a reasonable person would suffer
Only if π was in the zone of danger
cards.explanation: Psychological harm is always foreseeable when π suffers physical harm, and Δ is liable for all the psychological harm, even if that harm is unforeseeably severe.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'always foreseeable' is a categorical rule — no separate foreseeability inquiry once physical harm is present.

cards.scenario: Driver 1, proceeding lawfully, sees Driver 2 skidding toward him and accelerates to clear the point of entry rather than braking. Impact follows; braking would have been better. What result?
options: Negligent — the better response was available
Driver 1 may be found not negligent due to the emergency created by Driver 2; he is not required to exercise unerring judgment
Negligent unless he proves he could not have braked
Strictly liable
cards.explanation: The law does not hold one in an emergency to the exercise of that mature judgment required where there is opportunity for deliberate action, and he is not required to exercise unerring judgment. The emergency here was created by Driver 2, not Driver 1.
cards.why: Emergency protects defendants — but not one who created the emergency.

cards.scenario: Δ negligently sets a fire. π, a passerby, is injured rescuing Δ's child. Δ argues π's injury was unforeseeable. What result?
options: No duty — Δ could not have foreseen a rescuer
A duty runs to the rescuer — the wrongdoer may not have foreseen the coming of a deliverer, but he is accountable as if he had
No duty — rescuers assume the risk
A duty, but only if the rescue succeeded
cards.explanation: Danger invites rescue. A duty runs to the rescuer, often the same duty that ran to the primary π; the wrongdoer may not have foreseen the coming of a deliverer, but he is accountable as if he had. Cause in fact and proximate cause must still be established, but it is rare that harm to a rescuer is held too remote.
cards.why: Rescue makes plaintiffs — the mirror of emergency, which protects defendants.

cards.scenario: Δ negligently creates a risk to himself. π is injured attempting to rescue Δ. May π sue Δ?
options: No — one cannot be liable for endangering only oneself
Yes — a rescuer may sue the person rescued if that person is at fault for creating the risk
No — the rescue doctrine only protects the original π
Only if π's rescue attempt succeeded
cards.explanation: A rescuer may sue the person rescued, if that person is at fault for creating the risk. The doctrine runs against the person who created the danger, including where that person is the one rescued.
cards.why: TRICKY: the intuition that you cannot be liable for endangering only yourself is wrong here.

cards.scenario: π slips on a banana peel in Δ's store. The peel is brown and blackened. Which route to breach does that fact support?
options: Δ created the hazard
Constructive knowledge, based on the condition of the hazard
Actual knowledge
Res ipsa loquitur
cards.explanation: Δ is liable if it created the hazard, had actual knowledge of it, or had constructive knowledge. Constructive knowledge may be based on the condition of the hazard — brown banana peels are the outline's own example — or on the time between inspections.
cards.why: The color of the peel is doing the work: it shows the hazard was there long enough to be discovered.

cards.scenario: In a hazard and inspection case, who bears the burden on whether inspections were frequent enough?
options: Δ, because it controls the premises
π bears the burden
The burden shifts to Δ once a hazard is shown
Neither — it is a question of law
cards.explanation: In hazard and inspection cases the questions are whether inspections were made frequently enough and whether an inadequate inspection schedule caused the injury, and π has the burden.
cards.why: Stated expressly — do not assume premises control shifts the burden.

cards.scenario: π successfully pleads res ipsa. What has π established?
options: The entire prima facie case
Breach of duty for purposes of the prima facie case only — it gets π to the jury on duty and breach, does not bind the jury to accept the inference, and causation must be proven separately
A presumption Δ must rebut
Liability, subject to damages
cards.explanation: Res ipsa establishes breach of duty for purposes of the prima facie case only. It gets π to the jury on duty and breach but does not bind the jury to accept the inference, and causation must be proven separately.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'the thing speaks for itself' sounds conclusive; it only survives a directed verdict.

cards.scenario: π's new toaster oven bursts into flames on the third use, destroying so much of itself that the cause cannot be determined. Which requirement does the destruction of the evidence satisfy?
options: Exclusive control
That there is no direct evidence of precisely how the negligent act happened
That the accident does not normally occur absent negligence
Causation
cards.explanation: The first requirement is that there is no direct evidence of precisely how the negligent act happened — which is exactly the situation where the instrumentality destroys itself. π may plead res ipsa to establish breach of the manufacturer's duty.
cards.why: The absence of evidence is a requirement, not an obstacle.

cards.scenario: A surgical instrument is found inside π after an operation performed by a team Δ did not supervise or control. Which element is most in doubt?
options: That the accident does not normally occur absent negligence
That the instrumentality of injury was within Δ's exclusive control
That there is no direct evidence of how it happened
Duty
cards.explanation: Exclusive control is the element that fails where others handled the instrumentality. The other two requirements are comfortably met — instruments are not normally left inside patients absent negligence, and there is no direct evidence of how it happened.
cards.why: Exclusive control is usually the contested element in multi-actor cases.

cards.scenario: Who bears the burden on cause in fact, and what is the standard?
options: Δ, who must disprove causation
π — to offer evidence such that a reasonable jury could believe the breach more likely than not caused the harm for which this π sues
π, but only to a scientific certainty
Neither — it is presumed from breach
cards.explanation: π bears the burden: evidence such that a reasonable jury could believe the breach more likely than not caused the harm for which this π sues. It need not be quantifiable, and very often is not.
cards.why: Note 'this π' — general capacity to cause harm is not enough.

cards.scenario: π falls at night on an unlit staircase with no handrail. She cannot say why she fell but remembers reaching for a handrail that was not there. Δ argues she might have fallen anyway. What result?
options: π fails — she cannot say what caused the fall
π may reach the jury — the absence of a safety device may be inferred to be the cause in fact where the device is intended for precisely that purpose
π fails unless others also fell
π wins as a matter of law
cards.explanation: Where events are not quantifiable it is enough that the breach greatly multiplies the chances of accident and is of a character naturally leading to its occurrence. The absence of a safety device may be inferred to be the cause in fact when the device is intended for precisely that purpose — even though others did not fall and π might have fallen anyway.
cards.why: The reaching-for-the-handrail fact is what separates this from the 'I don't remember' failure.

cards.scenario: π's only testimony about the cause of her fall is 'I don't remember.' What result?
options: She reaches the jury — memory is not required
She fails — testimony insufficient to support any inference does not carry the burden
The burden shifts to Δ
Res ipsa supplies causation
cards.explanation: Testimony insufficient to support any inference fails. Contrast the staircase case, where π could not say why she fell but did remember reaching for an absent handrail — that fact supported the inference.
cards.why: TRICKY: the two fact patterns look alike; the difference is whether any inference is available.

cards.scenario: π establishes three possible causes of her harm, all attributable to Δ. There are no other possible causes, but as to none can it be said it is more likely than not. What result?
options: π fails — no single cause meets the standard
π still gets to the jury on cause in fact
The burden shifts to Δ to identify the cause
π must elect one theory
cards.explanation: Where π establishes three possible causes of harm, all attributable to Δ, and there are no other possible causes, π gets to the jury on cause in fact even though as to none can it be said that it is more likely than not.
cards.why: TRICKY: applying 'more likely than not' cause-by-cause gets this wrong — all roads lead to Δ.

cards.scenario: Δ's expert testifies to an alternative explanation but does not establish it is more likely than not. Is there a defect in Δ's position?
options: Yes — Δ's expert must establish Δ's explanation
No — Δ bears no burden of proof; the testimony is intended to dissuade the jury from accepting π's inference and is admissible as rebuttal
Yes — the testimony is inadmissible
No — because expert testimony is always conclusive
cards.explanation: Δ bears no burden of proof. Δ's expert testimony need not establish Δ's explanation; it is intended to dissuade the jury from accepting the inference offered by π's expert, and is admissible as rebuttal.
cards.why: Remember which party carries the burden before evaluating the evidence.

cards.scenario: The incidence of a disease in an unexposed population is 10 per 100,000. What must π prove about the exposed population?
options: More than 10 per 100,000
At least 21 per 100,000 — more than double the unexposed incidence
At least 15 per 100,000
At least 100 per 100,000
cards.explanation: π must offer expert testimony that the incidence of this type of harm in the exposed population is more than double the incidence in a similar unexposed population. Ten per 100,000 unexposed means at least 21 per 100,000 exposed — doubling gives 20, and π needs more than double.
cards.why: TRICKY: 'more than double' means 21, not 20 — the arithmetic is the trap.

cards.scenario: π's expert testifies the chemical is capable of causing her type of injury. Is that sufficient on cause in fact?
options: Yes — general causation is enough
No — π must prove the exposure caused HER injury, not merely that it can in general cause this type of injury
Yes — provided the exposure is proven
No — expert testimony is inadmissible on causation
cards.explanation: π must prove the exposure occurred AND that the exposure caused her injury — not that it can in general cause this type of injury. General capacity is not specific causation.
cards.why: Two distinct showings; general causation alone loses.

cards.scenario: What must be shown on cause in fact in a medical malpractice case?
options: That the physician deviated from the standard of care
That the physician's negligence more likely than not caused the death or loss, including loss of a chance of a better outcome
That the patient would certainly have survived
That the physician intended the harm
cards.explanation: In medical malpractice the physician's negligence must, more likely than not, have caused the death or loss — including loss of a chance of a better outcome.
cards.why: The loss-of-chance language expands what counts as the loss.

cards.scenario: Δ argues that because it can point to no precaution that would have prevented the harm, its activity cannot be abnormally dangerous. Which statement best analyzes the argument?
options: Δ is right — if no precaution would help, no duty can be imposed
Δ has it backwards — inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care is § 520(c), a factor pointing TOWARD abnormal dangerousness
Δ is right, because strict liability requires proof of an available precaution
The argument is irrelevant because § 520 lists elements, not factors
cards.explanation: Inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care is one of the § 520 factors, and it cuts in π's favor: Δ can be held liable even if not negligent. The impossibility of a precaution is part of why the activity is treated as abnormally dangerous, not a reason to exempt it.
cards.why: TRICKY: Δ's argument sounds like a negligence defense and is exactly inverted under § 520.

cards.scenario: Δ is threatened on a public sidewalk in Franklin and could safely walk away, but instead uses force. Does the privilege attach?
options: Yes — a majority of states no longer require retreat outside the home
No — retreat is required in Franklin and at common law outside the home, and safe retreat was available
Yes — doubts are resolved in favor of Δ
No — because Δ must always wait for the actual battery
cards.explanation: Retreat is required in Franklin and at common law. The exception is inside one's own home. On a public sidewalk with safe retreat available, the privilege does not attach.
cards.why: TRICKY: the national trend runs the other way, which is exactly why (a) is the trap. Franklin is a RETREAT jurisdiction.

cards.scenario: Of the § 520 factors, which is the single most important?
options: (a) a high degree of risk of some harm
(c) inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care
(e) inappropriateness of the activity to the place where carried on
(f) value to the community outweighed by dangerous attributes
cards.explanation: Inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care is the single most important of the § 520 factors — it is why the activity carries liability without fault in the first place. Be able to reproduce (a), (b), and (c); the full list is not required.
cards.why: Lead with (c) in an answer, then (a) and (b).

cards.scenario: Δ's conduct was arguably necessary in unusual circumstances, but it protected neither public property nor public health. Which defense should the answer reach for?
options: Public necessity — necessity is necessity
Justification — public necessity is almost always about protecting public property or quarantine protecting public health; most other circumstances point toward justification
Private necessity, with compensation owed
Self-defense
cards.explanation: Public necessity is almost always about protecting public property, or quarantine protecting public health. For most other circumstances, look toward justification — the catch-all recognizing that a privilege may arise in circumstances unanticipated before.
cards.why: TRICKY: the word 'necessary' in the facts pulls toward the necessity defenses; the sorting rule points elsewhere.

cards.scenario: You are writing the duty section of a negligence answer. Which statement is true of foreseeability?
options: It belongs only in proximate cause and should be left out of duty
Foreseeability is unavoidable in a duty case and must be addressed
It matters only where a statute supplies the duty
It is relevant only to the eggshell plaintiff rule
cards.explanation: Foreseeability is unavoidable in a duty case. It runs through the Hand analysis, the scope of the duty, and the type of harm — a duty section that never mentions it is incomplete.
cards.why: If you are writing about duty, you are writing about foreseeability.

cards.scenario: A guard sees a customer leave with unpaid goods and repeatedly calls for him to stop. Realizing the customer is a thirteen-year-old, the guard physically restrains him. Does the privilege attach?
options: No — physical restraint is never permitted
Likely yes — there was reasonable suspicion that goods were taken, and restraining a child after repeated demands is reasonable force to detain on the premises
No — a merchant must call the police instead
Yes — because a minor cannot refuse
cards.explanation: The privilege permits, upon reasonable suspicion that a customer has taken goods, reasonable and never deadly force to detain on the premises for a reasonable time to investigate. Repeated demands were ignored, and the amount of force reasonable against a thirteen-year-old is correspondingly modest.
cards.why: Run all three reasonableness checks: suspicion, force, and time.

cards.scenario: Same facts, except the guard grabs the boy, is kicked, and responds by slamming him to the ground. Which statement best analyzes the guard's position?
options: The privilege covers the whole encounter because the initial suspicion was reasonable
The privilege may attach to the initial detention but not to the slam — only reasonable, never deadly, force is privileged, and a privilege that attaches can be exceeded
The kick gives the guard an unlimited self-defense privilege
No privilege attaches at any point because the goods were never recovered
cards.explanation: Reasonable suspicion supports the initial detention with reasonable force. Slamming a child to the ground goes beyond reasonable force, and a privilege that properly attaches can still be exceeded. Self-defense against the kick would itself be limited to necessary force and carries no privilege to retaliate.
cards.why: TRICKY: the kick invites a self-defense answer — but there is no privilege to retaliate, and only necessary force is privileged.

cards.scenario: Which two elements function as the gatekeepers of an IIED claim?
options: Causation and severe emotional distress
Extreme and outrageous conduct, and the intentional or reckless mental state
Volitional act and causation
Severe emotional distress and the pre-existing condition rule
cards.explanation: Extreme and outrageous conduct and the intentional or reckless mental state are the gatekeeper elements — the screen a claim must pass. A vulnerable victim makes outrageousness easier to establish.
cards.why: Knowing which elements do the screening tells you where to spend your words.

cards.scenario: Two appellate courts of equal standing reach opposite conclusions on whether a publisher owed a duty for a classified ad, on materially identical facts. What does that illustrate?
options: One court plainly misapplied the formula
With the Hand formula a point can be made in either direction, because the comparison is social policy rather than arithmetic
